highlights: 2024, Italy submitted its Draft Budgetary Plan for 2025 to the Commission and to the Eurogroup. On that basis, the Commission adopts this opinion in accordance with Article 7 of Regulation (EU) No 473/2013, and 7. On 21 October 2024, upon the Commission recommendation on the economic, social, employment, structural and budgetary policies of Italy of 19 June 2024 6, the Council recommended Italy, in line with the requirements of the reformed Stability and Growth Pact, to limit the growth in net expenditure in 2025 to a rate consistent with, inter alia, putting the general government debt on a plausibly downward trajectory over the medium term and reducing the general government deficit below the 3% of GDP Treaty reference value. 8. On 15 October 2024, Italy submitted to the Commission its medium-term fiscal structural plan in line with Regulation (EU) 2024/1263 7. The plan commits to net expenditure growth not exceeding 1.3% in 2025, 1.6% in 2026, 1.9% in 2027, 1.7% in 2028 and 1.5% in 2029. The Commission has assessed the medium-term fiscal structural plan of Italy and recommends to the Council to adopt a recommendation setting the net expenditure growth ceilings contained therein. The Draft Budgetary Plan for 2025 is the first step in the implementation of the medium-term fiscal structural plan. 11. Based on the Commission’s estimates, the fiscal stance 10 is projected to be broadly neutral in 2025, by 0.1% of GDP, following a contractionary fiscal stance of 2.9% in 2024 related to the phase-out of the tax credit for housing renovations and of measures to mitigate the (economic and social) impact of high energy prices. This measure of fiscal stance appropriately considers the impact on aggregate demand of expenditure financed by non-repayable support (grants) from the Recovery and Resilience Facility and other EU funds. 12. According to the Draft Budgetary Plan, Italy’s general government deficit is projected to decrease to 3.3% of GDP in 2025 (3.8% in 2024) 11, while the general government debt-to-GDP ratio is set to increase to 136.9% at the end of 2025 (135.8% at the end of 2024), driven by the lagged impact on cash borrowing of the housing renovation tax credits accrued in the deficit until 2023. According to the Draft Budgetary Plan, net expenditure is projected to decline by 1.9% in 2024 and to increase by 1.3% in 2025. The growth rate of net expenditure in 2025 according to the Draft Budgetary Plan is the same as the growth rate in the medium-term fiscal structural plan submitted by Italy on 15 October 2024. In turn, according to the European Commission Autumn 2024 Forecast, Italy’s general government deficit is projected to decrease to 3.4% of GDP in 2025 (3.8% in 2024), while the general government debt-to-GDP ratio is set to increase to 138.2% at the end of 2025 (136.6% at the end of 2024). According to the European Commission Autumn 2024 Forecast, net expenditure is projected to decrease by 2.3% in 2024 and to increase by 1.3% in 2025. The main differences between both sets of projections for the debt-to GDP ratio reflect differences in nominal GDP growth both in 2024 and 2025. The risks to achieving the fiscal objectives for 2025 set out in the Draft Budgetary Plan 10 are tilted to the downside, and mainly relate to some of the announced measures on the expenditure side. 13. The Draft Budgetary Plan assumes that expenditure amounting to 0.6% of GDP will be financed by non-repayable support (“grants”) from the Recovery and Resilience Facility in 2025, compared to 0.3% of GDP in 2024. Expenditure financed by Recovery and Resilience Facility grants enables high-quality investment and productivity-enhancing reforms without a direct impact on the general government balance and debt of Italy. The Draft Budgetary Plan also assumes expenditure supported by loans from the Recovery and Resilience Facility, amounting to 1.3% of GDP in 2025, compared with 0.7% of GDP in 2024. 14. The Draft Budgetary Plan includes several policy measures with a fiscal impact in 2025. On the revenue side, these include the confirmation of the reduction of the tax wedge already implemented in 2024, although with a somewhat modified design. These permanent tax cuts are in part financed in 2025 by the remodulation of taxation on banks and insurance companies and other not yet specified measures. On the expenditure side, these measures include part of the reduction of the tax wedge (i.e. the new tax credit to low-wage employees which is recorded as social transfers), the allocation of funds for the renewal of the public sector wage contracts for the 2025-2027 period, new measures to support the households and natality, additional resources for the health sector and public investments, the extension of early retirement measures adopted in past years and targeted tax credits to support businesses which are financed, among others, by the revision of expenditures of ministries as well as local authorities and other not yet specified measures. According to Commission estimates, the overall additional impact of the revenue measures increases the government deficit by 0.3% of GDP in 2025. 15. According to the European Commission Autumn 2024 Forecast, Italy’s net expenditure is projected to increase by 1.3% in 2025, which corresponds to a cumulative growth of -1.0% in 2024 and 2025 taken together. The Commission is of the view that these net expenditure growth rates are in line with the Council recommendation of 21 October 2024 to limit the growth in net expenditure in 2025 to a rate consistent with putting the general government debt on a plausibly downward trajectory over the medium term and reducing the general government deficit below the 3% of GDP Treaty reference value. Those net expenditure growth rates would be appropriate initial steps towards the correction of the excessive deficit by 2026, as the Commission recommends to the Council to recommend to Italy. Moreover, those net expenditure growth rates would be appropriate initial steps towards the implementation of the medium-term fiscal structural plan. 16. According to the European Commission Autumn 2024 Forecast, nationally financed public investment is projected to increase to 3.4% of GDP in 2025 (from 3.3% of GDP in 2024). In turn, public expenditure on EU funded programmes, including Recovery and Resilience Facility grants, is expected to increase to 0.9% of GDP in 2025 (from 0.4% of GDP in 2024). 17. The Draft Budgetary Plan includes medium-term budgetary projections until 2027. The general government deficit is projected to decrease to 2.8% of GDP in 2026 and to 2.6% in 2027. Finally, the Council also recommended Italy to make the tax system more supportive to growth, with a focus on reducing the tax wedge on labour and in line with fiscal 19. The EU aggregate Chapter 1 shows that while overall short-term risks increased compared to the previous year, they remain well below the levels observed during the COVID-19 pandemic and the global financial crisis. The Commission’s early warning indicator S0 signals high short-term risks for Romania and Slovakia for 2025 (see Tables 1 and 2 for an overview). Short-term risks stem primarily from macroeconomic and financial vulnerabilities, including tight financing conditions in 2024, high current account deficits, high net international investment positions and low household saving rates in 2023. Moreover, both countries faced fiscal vulnerabilities, particularly due to their relatively high government deficits in 2024. Latvia is a borderline case: while the country faces to some extent financial vulnerabilities, its cyclically-adjusted balance exceeded the critical threshold only by a very narrow margin. Without this specific trigger, Latvia would be considered at low risk. An assessment of the S0 sub-components shows that fiscal vulnerabilities exist in six EU countries and vulnerabilities in the financial competitiveness domain in five EU countries. In the EU on average, gross financing needs – an important predictor for short-term fiscal sustainability risks – are expected to remain broadly unchanged at relatively high levels between 2024 and 2026. Debt repayments, followed by budget deficits, are the main drivers of gross financing needs in 2024 for most countries, while stock-flow adjustments are important for some countries. Different financial market indicators show that financing conditions in many EU countries eased somewhat in 2024, though remaining less favourable than prior to the last crises. Sovereign ratings are still favourable and stable on average across the EU, despite some differences across Member States. Chapter 2 shows that, for the EU as a whole, at unchanged fiscal policy, the debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to increase over the next 10 years, driven by gradual increases in the cost of ageing and in interest expenditure. In the baseline, the ‘r-g’ differential is assumed to remain only slightly negative by 2035, after increasing throughout the projection period mostly because of rising implicit interest rates. In the absence of fiscal consolidation, the favourable impact of this differential on debt dynamics – the ‘snowball effect’ – would therefore not be large enough to offset the increasing pressure from ageing costs on public finances. An alternative scenario shows that the increase in debt for the EU as a whole could be less pronounced if the structural primary balance converged back to the level of small deficit observed on average in the past 15 years (compared to the larger deficit assumed in the baseline). Conversely, a more limited fiscal adjustment, a less favourable ‘r-g’ differential or temporary financial stress would worsen the debt dynamics. The stochastic projections point to uncertainty around the baseline. With an 80% probability, debt will lie between 80% and 101% of GDP in the euro area as a whole by 2029, coming below its 2024 level (89.1% of GDP) with a 43% probability. In 2029, the debt ratio could stand above or below 91% with equal probability. High uncertainty in some countries reflects historically volatile macro-financial and fiscal conditions. Eleven Member States are found to be at high fiscal sustainability risks in the medium term (Belgium, Greece, Spain, France, Italy, Hungary, Austria, Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Finland). The high-risk classification is mainly driven by the debt dynamics under the no-fiscal-policy-change baseline, due either to currently high and still increasing debt ratios (Belgium, Spain, France and Italy), debt increasing beyond 90% of GDP (Austria, Poland, Romania, Slovakia and Finland), or debt declining but remaining at a high level and with only moderate room for additional consolidation by historical standards (Greece). In several cases, the stochastic analysis confirms the high risk of higher debt in 5 years’ time (Belgium, Spain, France, Italy, Austria and Finland) and shows significant uncertainty surrounding the baseline projections (Greece, Hungary and Romania). Vulnerability to more adverse assumptions, in particular in case of less favourable macro-financial conditions, also explains the classification (Hungary). Projected financing needs suggest that countries with the highest debt ratios could also be potentially exposed to liquidity challenges. At unchanged fiscal policy, medium-term fiscal sustainability risks are medium in nine Member States (Bulgaria, Czechia, Germany, Croatia, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Portugal and Slovenia). In five of these countries, debt is on an overall increasing trend and projected to reach by 2035 levels above 60% of GDP in the baseline (in Germany, Croatia, Latvia and Slovenia) and/or under more adverse conditions (in Lithuania, where stochastic analysis also points to a likely increase in debt). In two more countries – Bulgaria and Czechia – debt, although increasing, would remain under 60% of GDP under all scenarios but with either only moderate fiscal consolidation space by historical standards (Czechia) or high uncertainty on debt dynamics in the next 5 years, based on historical volatility (Bulgaria). Finally, two countries, namely Cyprus and Portugal, are deemed at medium risk despite a projected steady decline in debt. In the case of Cyprus, debt would fall well below 60% of GDP but subject to high uncertainty. For Portugal, the risk stems from the still elevated level of debt and the limited fiscal consolidation space by historical standards. In the remaining seven Member States (Denmark, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands and Sweden), medium-term fiscal sustainability risks are low, but with debt approaching 60% of GDP in some scenarios in the case of the Netherlands. Chapter 3 concludes that, at unchanged fiscal policy, four Member States face overall high long-term fiscal sustainability risks (Belgium, Luxembourg, Malta and Slovakia). The high-risk classification reflects a significant increase in ageing costs for all countries. For Belgium and Slovakia, also the unfavourable initial budgetary position contributes to the high fiscal effort required to ensure debt sustainability in the long term. Compared to the 2023 DSM, Slovenia improves from high to medium risk. For fourteen Member States, long-term fiscal sustainability risks are assessed as medium. Risks are primarily driven by the projected increase in ageing costs (Czechia, Germany, Ireland, Spain, Lithuania, Hungary, the Netherlands, and Slovenia), an unfavourable initial budgetary position (France, Poland and Romania) or both factors (Austria and Finland). In the case of Italy risks stem from the large fiscal adjustment that would be needed to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio to 60% by 2070. Compared to the 2023 DSM, Bulgaria goes from medium to low risk. The nine remaining Member States are considered to have low fiscal sustainability risks in the long term. Fiscal vulnerabilities slightly increased in the EU on average in 2024 compared with the previous year and exist in six countries (Italy, Austria, Belgium, France, Spain and Hungary, see Graph 1.3, Table 1.2). The vulnerabilities are primarily driven by declining but still elevated government deficits in 2024. Government debt also contributed to fiscal vulnerabilities as it declined but remained elevated in 2024 in nine countries, exceeding 100% of GDP in five countries. The interest rate-growth differential supported debt reduction, but to a lesser extent than in previous years. Government gross financing needs remained high in 2024 in five countries, even though the lengthening of average debt maturities in recent years mitigated short-term risks in several countries.

Meanwhile, other revenues which include non-tax revenues and fiscal resources carried forward from last year, is estimated to fall, reducing revenue by 2.5 percent of GDP. 25 The supplementary budget for FY2024, amounting to JPY 13.9 trillion, was enacted in Parliament on December 17, 2024. The bulk of the supplementary budget's impact is expected to affect FY2025, raising the fiscal deficit for that year by an additional 1.2 percentage points of GDP. 26 Specific policies include increasing wages for teachers, medical and health care workers, subsidies to support SMEs wage increase with additional financial support available for companies that offer training or invest in labor-saving technologies to enhance productivity alongside the wage hike, increased budget for childcare reflecting a focus 19. Japan faces several downside risks, stemming from both domestic and global changes in the economic and financial landscape. As a highly open economy and a leading global financial hub, Japan could be affected by and could have potential impact on global market volatility. In addition, external risks include a deterioration of global economic conditions, spillovers from aggressive protectionist policies of the incoming U.S. Administration, and spikes in commodity prices. Domestically, inflation presents both upside and downside risks. A slowdown in wage growth could undermine the BOJ’s efforts to achieve its inflation target. Conversely, a significant overshoot of inflation above its target could necessitate a sharp tightening of monetary policy, which may pose risks to households and businesses, especially those that are more vulnerable. Over the medium to long term, additional vulnerabilities include weakening fiscal discipline and rising interest rates that could challenge fiscal sustainability, escalation in geoeconomic tensions, low profitability among regional banks, the economic impact of an aging population, and the risks posed by natural disasters and extreme weather events. B.2 Longer-term Challenges and Vulnerabilities 24. Over the long term, an aging population will make it more difficult to manage Japan's very large public debt. Japan's aging population will lead to increasingly higher expenditures on pensions, healthcare, and long-term care, which will continue to strain public finances. In addition, a shift towards higher interest rates after a prolonged low interest rate environment is expected to make government debt servicing more costly. Given these long-term trends, which will further increase fiscal pressure, the continuation of large fiscal deficits and rising public debt will increasingly limit Japan’s fiscal space and challenge fiscal sustainability. This reduced flexibility will also hinder its ability to respond to future shocks, such as large-scale natural disasters. C.3 Strengthening Fiscal Prudence to Rebuild Fiscal Buffers 36. Given the spending pressures to cope with the needs of an aging population, a fiscal consolidation strategy that combines revenue mobilization with expenditure rationalization is critical to rebuilding fiscal buffers over the medium-term. In light of very high level of public debt and increasing fiscal spending pressures from Japan’s aging population, it would be prudent to improve the fiscal balance in order to rebuild fiscal buffers. An analysis of Japan’s public debt indicates that the threshold beyond which the government may face higher financing costs could be breached within the next decade (see Annex 4 “Debt Sustainability Analysis with Debt Threshold Extension). In this context, strengthening both revenue mobilization and expenditure efficiency are integral to fiscal consolidation strategy.

results.title: Debt Sustainability in Japan: Macroeconomic and Asset Pricing Perspectives
highlights: Abstract Debt sustainability has become increasingly important in advanced economies as they grapple with rising public debt levels, challenging monetary policies, and shifting investor expectations. This paper examines Japan’s fiscal position from the perspectives of the standard debt sus tainability analysis and the asset pricing approaches. The findings suggest that several factors contribute to mitigate debt sustainability risks. Moreover, under favorable conditions, the present value of government debt is consistent with its current market valuation, as it accounts for the country’s capacity to repay its debt relying on future primary surpluses and a reduction of its debt stock. However, as the Bank of Japan normalizes monetary policy and scales back from large scale bond purchases, the sustainability of Japan’s debt may come under increasing pressure. These findings underscore the importance of proactive fiscal adjustments to steer the economy towards long-term fiscal stability and enhanced resilience against financial shocks. from deflation would increase future debt servicing costs. Furthermore, as the Bank of Japan (BOJ) gradually scales back its purchases of Japanese government bonds and shifts the purchases back The public debt-to-GDP ratio was expected to decline until 2029 but would rise thereafter due to increasing expenditures from an aging population. Higher effective interest rates and lower GDP market value of debt—reaching ¥1,559 trillion and ¥1,375 trillion under the CDS and ERP discount rates, respectively—comfortably surpassing the market value of debt at ¥1,233 trillion. Moreover, the buffers are large enough to pay both the private debt holders as well as the BoJ. Under the optimistic scenario, the buffers are even larger - ¥2733 trillion and ¥2288 trillion under the CDS and ERP discount rates. To place these results in the context of the DSA, we computed the IRRs implied by the mar ket valuation of the debt (1.31 percent), the equity premium valuation (1.49 percent), and the CDS valuation (1.28 percent), all of which are very similar and about twice the value of the 0.7 percent ef fective interest rate reported in the AMRO DSA in 2024. The lower IRR in the DSA suggests that the government had previously issued debt at relatively low interest rates, keeping current debt servicing costs manageable. This difference is largely due to Japan’s prolonged low-interest-rate environment before 2022, which provided favorable borrowing conditions. However, the higher market-implied rates signal that new borrowing may come at a significantly higher cost than existing debt. Conse quently, as market rates continue to rise, the government could face increasing refinancing costs in the future. This is consistent with the projected effective interest rate that is expected to rise to 1.3 in 2033. In summary, our findings suggest that Japan’s fiscal position, while appearing precarious under the conservative assumption that only primary surpluses service debt, improves significantly when government assets are considered. The market value of debt aligns closely with its discounted cash flows, indicating investor confidence in Japan’s ability to meet obligations. This confidence likely stems from two key assumptions: that the government’s substantial asset holdings provide a backstop against default, and that debt held by the BOJ does not necessarily require redemption in the same manner as privately held debt. Under the optimistic scenario, fiscal space is evident, with government buffers far exceeding market debt values. These insights highlight the critical role of investor perceptions and policy flexibility in shaping Japan’s Japan, among advanced economies, has the highest debt-to-GDP ratio, which leads to examining whether its debt will be sustainable going forward. We studied this issue from two complementary perspectives, the conventional DSA approach and the asset pricing approach. The DSA suggested that the high public debt levels and gross financing needs, which currently exceed international benchmarks, have not yet posed substantial risks to debt sustainability because there are several mitigating factors, including the debt’s long-term maturities, little debt issued in foreign currency, and a stable domestic investor base. However, with public debt projected to increase steadily in both baseline and shock scenarios, the importance of gradual fiscal consolidation remains crucial. The asset pricing analysis suggested that under the authorities’ baseline scenario and assum ing that only primary surpluses are used to cover the debt service, complacency is not warranted: the discounted value of the primary surpluses and the long-term debt-to-GDP ratio target largely exceed the then–current market debt valuation. This could subject the country to the risk of a dras tic market correction if debt investors reprice their debt holdings and are forced to rebalance their portfolios. This adverse outcome, however, seems unlikely once government assets are included in the analysis as the fiscal outlook improves significantly. The resulting buffers after including government assets exceed the market value of the debt in both the baseline and optimistic scenarios, indicating a stronger financial position than previously assumed. This seemed to be the view of the market consensus: despite the high debt-to-GDP ratio, the country had always been able to roll over its debt with ease, and the market value of its debt was aligned with the discounted principal and coupon payments when discounted using the sovereign risk premia implied by the CDS market. Moreover, the buffers available to the government covered both the debt owed to the BoJ and private debt holders. Finally, under stress conditions it was likely that the government might defer payments to the BoJ to be able to pay back other debt holders first, which further contributed to the market view of JGBs as default-free assets. The seemingly sanguine market view should not be taken for granted, as investor sentiment can shift rapidly as market conditions change. This was evident in 2024 when changing investor sentiment triggered a massive unwinding of the yen carry trade (Aquilina et al. 2024, Shi and Pande 2024). In addition, according to Japan Ministry of Finance (2024), many of the government assets are either not readily marketable or could lose significant value in a fiscal crisis. Hence, steering the economy toward the optimistic scenario should remain a policy priority. Japan has benefited from stable debt dynamics supported by past central bank policies and strong domestic investor demand. However, these conditions should not be taken for granted. As the Bank of Japan gradually shifts away from its prolonged accommodative stance, rising interest rates could increase borrowing costs and introduce new fiscal challenges. Even if markets remain accommodative and tolerate deviations from fiscal fundamentals for an extended period, this will only amplify future risks. In the future, Japan’s ability to maintain debt sustainability will depend on a combination of pru dent debt management, revenue-enhancing strategies, and structural reforms. Incorporating gov ernment assets into fiscal planning strengthens Japan’s position, but maintaining investor confidence requires proactive measures. Transparent fiscal governance, clear communication with market par ticipants, and policies that promote long-term economic growth will be crucial to mitigating volatility. In conclusion, while Japan’s debt sustainability remains resilient for now, the evolving economic landscape necessitates continued vigilance. Policymakers must strike a delicate balance between maintaining fiscal credibility and managing economic growth, ensuring that Japan’s fiscal framework remains robust in the face of mounting global economic and geopolitical uncertainties.

results.title: Why Is Japan’s Government Debt So High? | St. Louis Fed
highlights: Japan’s government debt as a percentage of its gross domestic product (GDP) in 2023 was 195%, the highest share among major advanced economies. In this blog post, government debt refers to the total amount of government bonds issued by the central and local governments. The concept of public liability, on the other hand, encompasses not only debt but also other liability instruments, such as loans, held by a broader range of public institutions, including but not limited to social security funds and public financial institutions. As will become clear later, we argue that to analyze Japan’s fiscal situation, one must focus on the consolidated balance sheet of the public sector—considering both assets and liabilities—rather than the narrowly defined government debt. This high level of government debt mainly stems from decades of persistent fiscal deficits and near-zero economic growth, both largely driven by Japan’s aging population. By the mid-1970s, Japan’s fertility rate had fallen below the replacement rate of 2.1 children per woman. The fertility rate continued to decline steadily over subsequent decades. Combined with increased life expectancy, this trend placed Japan on a path to becoming a rapidly aging society. In 2001, the share of Japan’s population ages 65 and older was 18.4%. By 2024, this share had grown to 30.2%. Projections indicate this trend will continue, reaching 36.7% by 2045. (See the figure below.) As Japan’s population continues to age and its economic growth remains near zero, The combination of an aging population and a decline in overall population has resulted in a shrinking workforce, a key factor in Japan’s prolonged economic stagnation. See Jesús Fernández-Villaverde, Gustavo Ventura and Wen Yao’s 2025 article “ The Wealth of Working Nations,” in European Economic Review. the country faces a persistent fiscal challenge: a large social security deficit. The deficit increased from 4.1% of GDP in 1998 to 9.4% in 2011. In response, the Japanese government introduced major social security reforms in the early 2010s, notably under former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe. These reforms aimed to curb medical expenditures, adjust public pension contributions and payouts, and boost labor force participation among women and the elderly. These efforts managed to stabilize the growth of the social security deficit, but it remains substantial at 7.6% of GDP as of 2023. Due to the large social security deficit, Japan’s general government (which comprises the central and local governments) has consistently run a significant primary fiscal deficit, averaging 5.1% of GDP since 1998. Notably, the average primary deficit is smaller than the social security deficit, indicating that the government would have run a surplus if social security deficits were excluded. Fiscal consolidation efforts over the past decade, including consumption tax hikes in 2014 and 2019, have helped reduce the primary fiscal deficit but remain insufficient to balance the Japanese budget. As a result, financing Japan’s primary fiscal deficit has mainly relied on raising government debt, which increased from 70% of GDP in 1998 to 195% of GDP in 2023. As shown in the figure below, the trajectory of Japan’s general government debt closely mirrors that of its cumulative primary fiscal deficit. Japan’s high government debt is closely tied to a series of deliberate policy choices. First, to finance its large social security deficit, the Japanese government opted to issue bonds rather than draw down social security reserves. The social security reserves were invested in high-return, risky assets such as equities and foreign bonds, especially after 2012. As a result, despite persistent and significant social security deficits, the social security reserves grew over time—from 36% of GDP in 1997 to around 60% of GDP in 2023. Had the government used social security reserves to cover these deficits instead, the outstanding government debt would be significantly lower. Second, beyond bond issuance, the central and local governments have historically relied on alternative borrowing instruments, such as loans, or other borrowing channels, such as public financial institutions. Before 2000, the Japanese government borrowed heavily through the Fiscal Investment and Loan Program (FILP), a large government-run lending program. See Takero Doi and Takeo Hoshi’s article “ Paying for the FILP,” in Structural Impediments to Growth in Japan, National Bureau of Economic Research Inc., 2003, pp. 37-70. FILP served to finance various public investment projects through targeted loans and was primarily funded by Japan’s postal savings bank and social security fund. By the late 1990s, FILP’s loan portfolio had exceeded 100% of GDP. In the early 2000s, Japan began privatizing the postal savings bank, and FILP’s reliance on it for funding diminished. To sustain FILP operations, the Japanese government increasingly turned to the bond market, which further contributed to the growth of government debt. - An analysis of the public sector should not be limited to central and local governments. Other government agencies, such as FILP and the social security fund, should also be included. - Assessing overall liabilities requires examining debt securities as well as other borrowing instruments and channels, such as loans to FILP. - Government assets and investment portfolios also should be considered—for example, the risky asset holdings of the social security fund. In short, focusing solely on government debt can provide a distorted picture of public finances. Motivated by the above insights, YiLi Chien, Howard Cole and Hanno Lustig’s recent working paper consolidated the balance sheets of Japan’s central and local governments with those of other Japanese governmental agencies, including public pension funds, the Bank of Japan and public financial institutions. See “ What about Japan?,” Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Working Paper 2023-028C, revised in July 2024. The analysis produced several novel findings. - First, as of the second quarter of 2024, Japan’s net public liabilities on the consolidated balance sheet amounted to only 78% of GDP. While gross liabilities stood at 270% of GDP, the government also held substantial assets totaling 192% of GDP. - Second, a significant portion of these assets were invested in high-return, riskier assets such as domestic equities, foreign equities and foreign bonds. Liabilities primarily consisted of low-return instruments like bank reserves and government bonds. This resulted in a return spread between government assets and liabilities. Despite having a net liability position, the high returns on riskier assets exceeded the government’s funding costs, generating a substantial positive return on Japan’s balance sheet. The analysis showed Japan’s public sector balance sheet earned an annual return that exceeded its funding costs by exceeding 6% of GDP between 2013 and 2023. The large annual net return explains why Japan’s net liabilities have increased at a much slower rate than its government debt.

results.title: Scope ratings
highlights: Japan’s sovereign Outlook was revised to Stable from Negative on 22 March due to higher inflation and its positive effects on debt sustainability. Very high levels of public debt, weak growth and rising ageing-related costs remain constraining factors. The Stable Outlook reflects a balanced view of risks to the ratings over the next 12-18 months. Japan’s long-term issuer and senior unsecured debt ratings in local and foreign-currency were affirmed at A. The local and foreign currency short-term issuer ratings were affirmed at S-1. The Outlook on short-term ratings remains Stable. s recent inflation appears increasingly . Headline and core inflation rose to 2.8% year-on-year as of February 2024 whereas Tokyo inflation, a bellwether of the national index, stayed elevated last month. Annual headline inflation at the national level has stayed above 2.0% since April 2022, evidencing a degree of stickiness after government reflation policies of the past decade under Abenomics were given a significant boost from the global cost-of-living crisis. Inflation in Japan was negative for 12 of the 27 years between 1995 and 2021 and under 2% in all but one of those years (Figure 1). This record of deflation – so-called Japanification – has represented a core constraint for government debt sustainability and a limitation on the economy’s real output growth. While it is too early to declare victory over deflation, the phase of higher inflation of the past two years looks increasingly durable. We are projecting inflation of 2.2% for 2024 and 2.5% for 2025. oring inflation closer to 2% in since medium-run inflation risk remains skewed to the downside given structural deflationary dynamics The stronger inflation outlook is constructive for the challenging debt-sustainability outlook. Under our economic base case, a comparative stabilisation of the government-debt ratio is forecast over 2024-2028. We are forecasting debt-to-GDP of 255% by 2028, roughly unchanged from 253% at end-2023. Elevated nominal growth of 5.8% last year brought about a reduction of the debt ratio from record highs of 260% in 2022, the largest one-year drop on record. Our debt outlook is anchored by more-constructive nominal growth compared to nominal interest rate differentials than in previous years (Figure 2), driven by higher inflation. Japan is among a select number of sovereigns (including Greece) that have been helped significantly from a credit standpoint by the cost-of-living crisis. High inflation has cut elevated debt ratios after many debt-reduction strategies of past decades proved less effective, while low-interest and long-maturity debt structures have aligned with more significant space for higher borrowing rates. Net interest payments amounted to a low 0.5% of Japan’s government revenue in 2023 and we foresee net interest payments rising gradually to a still-modest 2% by 2028 under an assumption of higher rates for longer. So although Japan holds the highest debt ratio of any rated sovereign State, it pays among the least interest of Scope’s sovereign universe. The effective interest rate on remains stays near 0% within our forecast horizon to 2028. Debt sustainability is also supported by the fact that Japan’s debt is predominantly domestically held, denominated entirely in yen, and 48% has been monetised by the Bank of Japan. Because of the latter fact, the amount of rateable debt due to the private sector is much lower than the sovereign’s gross debt ratio. Although the BoJ ended yield-curve control recently, it continues purchasing bonds in secondary markets broadly as before, ensuring further rises of the share of government debt it holds. Finally, as the world’s largest creditor nation, Japan holds gross government financial assets of around 96.7% of GDP (IMF, 2023), nearly equal in size to gross debt due to the private sector. On this basis, the aggregate debt-sustainability picture is more benign than the sovereign’s very-elevated debt ratio alone might suggest.

results.title: Separating Fact from Fear in Japanese Investing
highlights: Japan is often labeled a ticking time bomb due to its high level of debt and bleak fiscal outlook. Recently, fears have emerged around rising Japanese Government Bond (JGB) yields triggering a global financial meldtown. In our view, these fears are exaggerated. In this piece, we aim to clarify and correct some common myths around the Japanese economy and investment universe. There are concerns about Japan’s fiscal stability, and there are worries that rising JGB yields will trigger massive repatriational damage and foreign bond outflows. We point to various fundamental factors supporting Japan’s fiscal picture, and explain the structural nature of Japanese holdings of US Treasury bonds (USTs). Myth: Japan’s economy is a ticking time bomb due to its 250% debt-to-GDP ratio. Reality: On a net basis, Japan’s debt-to-GDP (around 140% 1 ) is far lower and more manageable than the 250% gross ratio (Figures 1 and 2). It is critical to assess a country’s debt net of its financial assets, rather than rely solely on gross figures. The Japanese government holds substantial assets—including large foreign reserves, assets held by quasi-public banks, and pension funds—that offset its liabilities. The gross debt-to-GDP ratio was roughly 240% in 2024, down from 250% in 2020. However, net debt-to-GDP of 140% in 2024 was an improvement from 160% in 2020. Moreover, Japan remains one of the world’s largest net creditor nations, with net external assets totalling ¥533 trillion (approx. $3.7 trillion) in 2024.2 This, combined with the government’s sizable asset base, paints a far more stable fiscal picture than the gross debt may suggest. Myth: Japan’s policymakers risk losing control of the long end of the JGB curve due to fiscal worries. Reality: Japan’s large, stable domestic investor base and the country's ability to remain self-financed for decades continue to anchor long-term JGB stability. While elevated yields typically reflect rising global borrowing costs amid concerns over fiscal deterioration, Japan’s case is different. The recent weakness in the super-long end of the JGB curve reflects technical supply-demand imbalances and market dysfunction—not a fundamental shift in fiscal outlook. Japan’s fiscal picture remains structurally sound, as the country has a large and stable domestic investor base, and it is able to remain self-financed for decades (roughly 90% of JGBs are held domestically).3 Household financial assets are nearly twice the size of national debt. For more insight, see Japanese Super-Long Bond Weakness: Why We’re Not Sounding the Alarm Bells Just Ye t). Given these factors, the risk of Japanese policymakers losing control of the long end of the yield curve is extremely low, and concerns over a sharp JGB selloff appear overstated. Not to mention that compared to the US, where gross debt-to-GDP is 120% and net is 96%, Japan is unique in having reduced its debt-to-GDP ratio since 2020 (Figure 3). This improvement reflects a combination of stronger GDP growth and higher interest income from Japan’s substantial $3.7 trillion in net external assets. Japan remains the only advanced economy to show a meaningful decline in debt burden over this period. Myth: JGB weakness portends a global financial meltdown. Reality: Japan’s US Treasury holdings are structural. Investors are more likely to tap idle yen cash before selling foreign bonds. Rising JGB yields do not imply a capital repatriation wave or a situation in which Japanese investors are pulling funds from the US, ultimately leading to global market disruption. We believe that concerns of massive repatriation and capital outflows from the US are not warranted because Japan’s US Treasury holdings are structural. 1. Japanese life insurers. MOF data shows that Japanese life insurers already reduced their foreign bond exposure (especially USTs) during the 2022~23 Fed hiking cycle (Figure 5). We see limited risk of further selling, though near-term demand remains soft. That said, technical conditions should improve for Asian investors, as the UST curve steepens under a Fed easing cycle and as the term premium reprices. In general, lower hedge costs plus a higher pickup in back-end spreads is a formula that could lead to increased international demand for US bonds—especially in corporate bonds, which offer a spread pickup over Treasury rates. 2. Japanese banks. These asset owners hold ample cash at the BOJ, having sold JGBs during past Quantitative Easing phases. As yields rise, their first line of defense will likely be reallocating this cash into JGBs, before selling foreign assets (Figure 4). 3. Foreign reserves and public pension funds. These holdings are structural and rooted in Japan’s strategic alliance with the US (see: Are Foreign Investors Really “Dumping” US Treasury Bonds?). The Bottom Line We believe that excessive concerns that Japan’s fiscal situation will lead to a broader financial market downturn are unwarranted. Japan’s debt burden is often overstated, with gross debt cited at 250% of GDP. However, the net debt level is closer to 140%, which is far more manageable. In addition, Japan benefits from a stable domestic investor base that helps to anchor the long-term JGB market. The risk that rising JGB yields could trigger a broader selloff in USTs is also overstated, as structural factors continue to underpin market stability.

highlights: The US and Europe are working on a joint plan to end the war, according to a column in The Washington Post. American negotiators are trying to put together a **package** that addresses the postwar needs of both Ukraine and Russia. It is intended to stop the bloodshed and help both sides agree to a territorial compromise that neither will like. According to the US official, t **he package will have four main components**. The message to Russian leader Vladimir Putin should be this: do not simply stop the war with Ukraine, but conclude an economic and security agreement with Europe. The idea is that this would restore stability in the region. **Ukraine's reconstruction**. The World Bank and investment firm BlackRock want to establish a framework to cover Kyiv's financial needs. This includes rebuilding destroyed areas, assisting the families of fallen and wounded military personnel, and restoring the economy. The negotiators asked Kyiv to provide a detailed cost estimate and guarantees that the money would not be plundered by postwar speculators. The Ukrainians have not yet submitted the figures. They are expected to do so within the next few days, **Security guarantees**. Ukraine will receive commitments from the US and European countries to respond militarily if Russia attacks again. The official described this as equivalent to Article 5 of NATO, which establishes collective defense: an attack on one alliance member is considered an attack on all. **Energy agreement**. The third area is the economic integration of Russia, Ukraine, and Europe. One possible element is a pipeline supplying Russian oil and gas to Europe. Ukraine and Russia would share the profits from it. According to the official, such a pipeline could sharply reduce Europe's energy costs. In addition to granting Russia "long-term access to the European energy market," the peace agreement would determine how and when the existing economic sanctions would be lifted. **Territory**. The final part of the agreement concerns the front line. Russia, which launched the war hoping to seize all of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the current front line. The negotiators call it the "line of control." For Ukraine, this would mean that Russia would control the occupied territories, including Donbas, which is at the center of a fierce dispute. results.title: U.S. plans new Ukraine peace package, The Washington Post says / The New Voice of Ukraine
highlights: U.S. and Europe draft new four-point Ukraine peace plan including security guarantees and ceasefire The United States plans to advance a new peace package for Ukraine covering reconstruction, security guarantees, a ceasefire along the front line and energy agreements, The Washington Post reported, citing sources on Oct. 13. “The United States and Europe are slowly moving toward a joint peace proposal that [the U.S. administration believes] would provide financial and security benefits to both Ukraine and Russia and form the basis for a territorial settlement that would not fully meet either side's military objectives,” Washington Post columnist David Ignatius wrote, citing his sources, including U.S. officials. According to a U.S. official, the proposed package consists of four main elements. The first is Ukraine's reconstruction. The World Bank and investment firm BlackRock are seeking to establish a mechanism to meet Ukraine's financial needs for rebuilding devastated areas, supporting the families of service members killed or wounded in the war, and restoring the economy. The second element involves security guarantees. Under the proposal, Ukraine would receive assurances from the United States and European countries that they would respond with military measures in the event of another Russian attack. A U.S. official described the arrangement as similar to NATO's Article 5 collective defense provision. The third element could involve economic integration among Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy agreement. One aspect of the plan could be a pipeline transporting Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia sharing the profits. According to the U.S. official, such a pipeline could significantly reduce Europe's energy costs. In addition to providing Russia with “long-term access to the European energy market,” the peace agreement would establish how and when existing economic sanctions would be lifted. The final element, however, would be the “most difficult to accept,” The Washington Post reported. According to sources, the United States and Europe expect Moscow to agree to a ceasefire along the front line, which negotiators refer to as the “line of control.” This would mean Ukraine would have to accept Russian control over occupied territories, including parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.

highlights: I don’t know why this wasn’t above-the-fold news all across the country over the past few days as the details of the “peace plan” Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff took to Putin this week came out. The brutal kingdom of Saudi Arabia owns agricultural land in many far-flung places, from their alfalfa farms in Arizona to an investment in 400,000 acres in Western Ukraine devoted to growing grain for export. The only way to get that grain to the Black Sea where it can enter world markets is via barges down the Dnieper River, which cuts across Ukraine. “Point 23 of the peace plan that Kushner helped draft fulfills Saudi’s policy objective: ‘Russia will not prevent Ukraine from using the Dnieper River for commercial activities, and agreements will be reached on the free transport of grain across the Black Sea.’” So, it probably shouldn’t surprise us that Jared, after taking $2 billion from the Saudis along with his $25 million/year “fee,” would insert a paragraph into the Russia/Ukraine deal that would benefit the Saudi crown prince who’s been his top benefactor. And, even more astonishing, that he is serving in this position without any legal authority in violation of federal law. As Judd Legum explains, if he’s a private individual it’s a felony crime for him to negotiate with a foreign government, and if he’s acting on behalf of our government he’s a “special government employee” and therefore subject to the Emoluments Clause. results.title: NATO commander outlines “block, blunt, break” doctrine to deter Russian aggression – EUalive
highlights: NATO’s top military commander on Monday laid out a clear doctrine for defeating any potential Russian assault on Alliance territory, declaring that forces would move swiftly to block an initial strike, blunt any advance, and ultimately break the adversary’s ability to continue fighting. Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe, described the approach as a shared “Theory of victory” designed to convince Moscow that attacking any of the 32 allies would prove utterly futile. The remarks came against a backdrop of heightened tensions, including reported Russian sabotage, drone incursions and cyber operations across Europe, lingering doubts about American resolve under President Donald Trump, and Russia’s recent nuclear warnings tied to its Kaliningrad exclave. Grynkewich summarized the concept in three stages: block, blunt and break. In the first phase, ground forces would dominate the strike at the point of contact and pin down enemy formations through maneuver. Air, naval, space and cyber forces would simultaneously secure superiority and freedom of action, stripping the adversary of the ability to hold any captured positions. The second stage focuses on blunting ongoing or subsequent assaults through advanced sensors, autonomous systems and coordinated multi-domain operations designed to prevent the attacker from gaining momentum or seizing the initiative. If the adversary nevertheless continues the attack or commits reserves, the Alliance would shatter the entire system of warfare employed against it, striking the structures that support, supply and enable the enemy to direct operations. This would be achieved by combining advanced precision-guided munitions with large numbers of low-cost, scalable systems while maintaining constant pressure across all domains. The result would cut the enemy off from reinforcements, deprive commanders of control and destroy their remaining capabilities. The military commander explained that executing this scenario does not require inflicting a strategic defeat. The Alliance wants only to deter attack and deny the aggressor the ability to seize and hold territory. This demands defeating the forces arrayed against NATO at the tactical and operational levels and dismantling the adversary’s warfighting system so that further aggression becomes impossible. Full moral, political and strategic responsibility for any attack would rest solely with the aggressor, who must understand that the advantage lies with the Alliance and that escalation would only worsen their position both militarily and politically. The threat of escalation, or even actual escalation during a conflict, would not break the Alliance. On questions of unity and American commitment, Grynkewich was direct. He recalled the atmosphere at a NATO summit earlier in the year and took the unanimous reaffirmation of Article 5 by all 32 allies at face value. Evidence of unity, he argued, lies in the fact that debate has moved past whether Europe must do more or whether a “NATO 3.0” is required; the Alliance is now in the implementation phase. The plan accounts for the possibility that U.S. forces could be engaged elsewhere, including in the Indo-Pacific. European officials have privately echoed that assessment, stating they expect American support but are prepared to fight with or without it if necessary. On escalation, Grynkewich was unambiguous. Threats or actual moves up the ladder – nuclear or otherwise, would not fracture the Alliance. NATO retains the ability to deliver mass effects and match any adversary’s escalatory steps. The message he left was deliberate and blunt: NATO knows how it will fight if war comes, and it knows it will win. Significantly, Grynkewich affirmed that threats or actual escalation – including nuclear saber-rattling – would not fracture the alliance and that NATO could match any move up the escalation ladder, including with its nuclear capabilities, taking “comfort in our ability to deliver mass effects.” This framing leaves open the classic risk that a conventionally failing Russia could still choose nuclear use as a last resort to reverse battlefield setbacks, a contingency Grynkewich addressed mainly through alliance cohesion and matched deterrence rather than detailed public warfighting plans. General Alexus Grynkewich presented a new NATO theory of victory at the Warsaw Security Forum 2026, built around three pillars aimed at convincing any potential aggressor that an attack on an alliance member would fail to achieve its objectives. Grynkewich said NATO remains a defensive alliance that does not seek war, but stressed that its defensive character should not be mistaken for weakness. He said the alliance seeks deterrence and peace through collective strength, but that any attacker would face a fight intended to stop the assault and deny it any of its intended outcomes. The framework rests on three elements described by Grynkewich as "blunt the initial attack," "block continuation of attack," and "degrade the enemy." The second pillar addresses stopping an offensive once it has begun. Even if an aggressor achieved initial, localized success, NATO intends to block further advances and prevent any lasting occupation of allied territory. Grynkewich said the alliance would not allow an adversary to maintain a foothold on NATO territory. The third pillar involves degrading the aggressor's military potential to a point where it can no longer sustain operations. This requires striking enemy forces in ways that strip away their capacity to continue an effective campaign. Grynkewich emphasized cooperation across operational domains and the combination of precision weaponry with systems capable of large-scale operations, noting that defense effectiveness depends not only on the number of weapons systems available but on their interoperability and coordinated application against an adversary. The alliance aims to adapt its response to an aggressor's actions on the escalation ladder, while keeping its core objective focused on halting attacking forces rather than pursuing offensive action for its own sake. highlights: As [reported](https://nos.nl/artikel/2634678-hoogste-navo-militair-bij-aanval-vijand-tegenhouden-afzwakken-en-breken) by the Dutch broadcaster NOS, General Alexus Grinkevich outlined the alliance's strategy at the security summit in Warsaw. His speech was previously announced as a presentation of the "theory of victory" over Russia, although during the speech itself, the general did not mention Russia by name. ## “If someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight” Grinkevich clearly described NATO's course of action in the event of a military attack. "We will stop the enemy's attack, weaken it if it continues to advance, and ultimately incapacitate its operational combat system," the general stated. He emphasized that he hopes to never face the necessity of implementing such a scenario. According to the commander, his speech is primarily aimed at deterring a potential adversary and strengthening the confidence of allies. "At this moment, the conflict is neither inevitable nor imminent," he explained. Grinkevich reminded several times that the North Atlantic Alliance is a defensive organization. "But if someone is foolish enough to attack us, we will fight," the general warned. ## NATO speaks openly about victory strategy for the first time The public speech of the highest operational commander of the alliance explaining the strategy for conducting a possible war is quite an unusual event. Typically, such issues are discussed behind closed doors in military headquarters. However, this time NATO leadership decided to openly demonstrate the alliance's readiness to repel possible aggression. The speech took place against the backdrop of increased hybrid attacks against NATO member states, which are suspected to be linked to Russia. These include, in particular, sabotage and other actions aimed at destabilizing the situation and spreading panic. Such operations put NATO in a difficult position: to respond to provocations or to show restraint to prevent individual incidents from escalating into a full-scale conflict. In this context, Grinkevich's speech was meant to demonstrate that the alliance has a strategy not only for defense but also for defeating the enemy in case of an attack. ## “We will manage”: the general addressed a billion residents of NATO countries The American military leader paid special attention to the issue of trust in the alliance. During a conversation with summit participants after his speech, he stated that he wants to reassure the population of NATO countries. "I want to show all one billion residents of NATO states: we will manage," Grinkevich said, using the English expression *we got this*. He was also asked about the threats that keep him awake at night. The general's response was quite confident. "None. My job is to keep others awake at night," he stated. ## Zelensky had to hear conflicting signals However, the American general's speech came against a backdrop of ambiguous signals from Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was also present at the summit in Warsaw. As noted by NOS, just a few days before Grinkevich's speech, news emerged about the United States' plans to begin importing Russian oil and diesel fuel. It is assumed that such supplies are intended to help lower prices at American gas stations ahead of the midterm elections in November. Thus, on one hand, NATO's top military leadership demonstrates readiness to confront possible Russian aggression, while on the other, Washington is taking steps to expand energy trade with Russia. Additional tension is created by statements from U.S. President Donald Trump. According to NOS, over the past weekend, the American leader again sharply criticized Zelensky, stating that Ukraine needs a new president capable of reaching an agreement. Moreover, the publication claims that Trump threatened to halt arms supplies to Ukraine through NATO mechanisms. Previously, the U.S. president had repeatedly made statements that raised questions about the extent of American commitment to the North Atlantic Alliance. ## The U.S. is not going to abandon NATO, the general assured Amid these contradictions, Grinkevich specifically addressed the role of the United States in the collective defense system. The general, appointed to his position under President Trump, assured allies of the unwavering American commitments. "No one should have any reason to doubt the United States' commitment to this alliance," he stated. This statement became one of the key political signals of the speech. In fact, the American commander attempted to simultaneously address two tasks: to warn a potential adversary of the consequences of an attack and to convince European allies that the U.S. remains a crucial support for NATO. ## Deterrence instead of war Despite the harsh wording, the main message of Grinkevich's speech was not about the inevitability of military confrontation, but about the necessity of preventing it. According to NATO leadership's plan, a potential adversary must understand that an attack on the alliance will not bring it military victory. At the same time, the public explanation of the strategy is intended to demonstrate the allies' resolve and reduce the risk of miscalculations by a potential aggressor. For Latvia and other Baltic states, these statements hold particular significance. Against the backdrop of ongoing tensions on NATO's eastern borders, the words of the supreme commander represent a direct assurance of the alliance's readiness to defend its members. However, there remains a noticeable tension between military guarantees and conflicting political signals from Washington.

(Bradley Latham/Stars and Stripes) NATO would seek to defeat invading Russian forces, sever their supply lines and cripple their command systems, but stop short of pursuing a wider war under a new strategy unveiled Monday by the alliance’s top commander. U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich publicly outlined his Theory of Victory during a security forum in Warsaw, Poland, where he said the alliance would counter an attack on its territory with overwhelming force while limiting the risk of a broader military conflict. “Should the adversary choose to press the attack or commit his reserves, we will break the warfighting system engaged against us,” Grynkewich said. “This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains or controls that force.” Grynkewich said he decided to publicly unveil his Theory of Victory, which was finalized in classified form about three months ago, to address growing anxiety inside the 32-member NATO alliance. The theory involves three actions: block, blunt and break, Grynkewich said. First, NATO ground forces would move to stop an invasion at the point of attack, preventing an enemy from quickly seizing territory and presenting the alliance with a fait accompli, he said. Air and naval forces, supported by space and cyber capabilities, would simultaneously seek control of the battlefield, allowing NATO to bring overwhelming firepower against advancing formations, Grynkewich said. If the assault continued, NATO would move to blunt the offensive by using advanced sensors, drones and coordinated attacks to prevent enemy forces from gaining momentum. The final phase would involve dismantling the military system supporting the invasion, including its logistics, communications and command structures, he said. “We will apply constant and unyielding pressure, both kinetic and non-kinetic,” Grynkewich said. “We will do this across and through domains: land, air, sea, space and cyberspace.” The result would be enemy formations deprived of reinforcements and supplies, commanders unable to control their troops, and attacking forces progressively destroyed, he said. However, NATO’s attack would be focused on defeating the forces involved in an invasion and the military systems supporting them, rather than pursuing Russia’s broader strategic defeat, he said. “In executing what I’ve outlined above, we are not seeking to impose a strategic defeat on our adversary. Nor do we need to do so,” he said. Grynkewich argued that any attempt by Russia to escalate would only strengthen NATO’s unity and worsen Moscow’s military and political position. “We should take comfort in our ability to deliver mass effects and the implicit warning that we could match any enemy move up the escalation ladder,” Grynkewich said. The theory comes as NATO faces persistent questions about whether it is prepared to rise to the challenge if tested by Russia. While NATO’s bedrock collective defense provision, known as Article 5, calls for a collective response in the event of an attack, there are concerns that some allies could balk. Grynkewich refuted the notion that allies would hesitate if challenged, pointing to the commitment to Article 5 reaffirmed by all 32 allies at their recent summit in Turkey. Meanwhile, Grynkewich said NATO must be prepared for a conflict in Europe even if American forces are simultaneously engaged elsewhere, including the Indo-Pacific. While NATO is prepared to “fight tonight,” Grynkewich said that preparing for war did not mean he expected one. “I do not assess that conflict is imminent or inevitable. results.title: IMF Warns of Cyber Threats to Finance and AI Market Correction
highlights: IMF Warns of Cyber Threats to Finance and AI Market Correction Cyber threats pose an ‘elevated’ risk to the global financial system, the IMF warned on Tuesday, during its annual meetings, in Bangkok. The IMF issued warnings on Tuesday, saying cyber threats pose “elevated” risks to the financial system. It also voiced concern over the chance of a market correction related to AI. Both could have “severe” consequences, it said. “These risks are plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil,” the report said. The recent boom in artificial intelligence – and the related rush to manufacture semiconductors and build data centres – has provided a boost to global growth despite geopolitical pressures including the Middle East war. However, “growing evidence suggests that AI capabilities can be delivered at lower investment levels… or that potential economic gains may not be as large as expected,” the IMF warned. “Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction.” And while AI is increasingly a source of economic vitality globally, it is also presenting unprecedented risks, the Fund said. “Severe cyber incidents could undermine market confidence and disrupt critical financial market infrastructure and operations,” it said. As AI capabilities continue to improve, the risk of successful cyberattacks on “critical financial institutions or market infrastructure” is getting “worse”, the IMF report said. Another growing risk to the global financial system is a spike in bond yields, which could trigger severe shocks due to the “foundational importance of sovereign bond markets”, the report said. “Bond markets are susceptible to further rises in energy prices re-igniting inflation and forcing the tightening of monetary policy.” Debt at sky-high levels The Fund forecast that global growth this year would slow less than previously expected because advanced economies were showing “resilience” despite the rise in energy prices caused by the war in the Middle East. But it said low-income countries were vulnerable to a supply shock. With global debt-to-GDP ratios at sky-high levels, including in advanced economies, the IMF has called on governments to cut spending and manage borrowing – a difficult task for those in the developing world struggling with the Iran war shock. The United States’ war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran’s retaliation. Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95% above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity. Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a “bifurcated outlook” in its WEO report. The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a “fragmented” world economy. “Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest,” it said. The IMF’s split view of the world economy was evident The Middle East and Central Asia region – exposed directly to the Iran war – is expected to suffer a 0.3% contraction in 2026. Saudi Arabia’s is one of the worst affected, with its economy projected to shrink 3.3% – a 5% cut in Fund’s forecast. In advanced economies, growth fuelled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong. The world’s advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1% in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain, such as Taiwan and South Korea, posting significantly higher figures. But growth in China, the world’s second-largest economy, was expected to slow, the IMF said, because of weak domestic demand. Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7% in 2026, with effects spread across advanced and developing economies. Asia’s tech-heavy markets slumped on Tuesday on fresh worries about the outlook for the AI investment boom, while European stocks gained thanks to a retreat in oil prices.

results.title: IMF warns an AI stock correction could threaten global financial stability - Startup Fortune
highlights: The IMF's stress test found banks holding 22% of global banking assets now show weak capital levels, up from 18% a year ago, while $1.4 trillion in hyperscaler-AI financing deals sit largely off public markets. s Global Financial Stability Report, out October 13, puts a hard number on the danger: seven companies now make up more than 35% of the S&P 500's value, and $1.4 trillion in future revenue is riding on deals between hyperscalers and AI firms that may not be able to pay. The International Monetary Fund has spent most of 2026 talking about AI as a growth story. On Tuesday, in its October Global Financial Stability Report, it switched to talking about AI as a risk to the plumbing of the financial system itself. The Fund's language is specific: a correction in AI-linked equities and credit, if it comes, "could trigger a market correction" that spreads well beyond tech stocks. What makes this different from a normal tech rally is how the money actually moves. The IMF's report tracked fourteen publicly disclosed deals since 2023 in which hyperscalers, the Microsofts and Amazons and Googles of the world, have put roughly $300 billion of equity into financially weaker AI companies, backed by another $650 billion in debt. In return, the hyperscalers have locked in $1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments, mostly through chip orders and cloud service contracts. That is the structure Kristalina Georgieva's economists are worried about: a handful of giants extending credit and equity to partners whose ability to pay depends entirely on AI demand materializing on schedule. The IMF's own stress test offers some comfort and some new worry. Banks representing 22% of global banking assets showed weak capital levels under a severe scenario combining an AI shock, a bond market shock and an energy shock, up from 18% in the Fund's 2025 assessment. That is a one-year jump in fragility, not a collapse. The headline finding is still that the core banking sector holds up. The leverage has moved somewhere else . Hedge funds' combined gross equity positions and margin loans have climbed from about 10% to roughly 15% of advanced-economy GDP, the report found, and the share of single packed into leveraged exchange-traded funds has jumped from 16% to 28% as retail investors chase amplified exposure to AI names. is where a correction would actually bite first: not insured deposits, but margin calls and levered ETFs that retail money has piled into without necessarily knowing it. Speaking ahead of the s annual meetings she warned that earnings fall short, "hypers leverage and large and growing could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock saying some U to levels seen at the peak of the dot Frankly, the Fund isn't predicting a crash. It is doing something more useful: pricing the collateral damage if one happens. IMF modeling has warned that a moderate correction in AI stock valuations, combined with tighter financial conditions, could reduce global growth by 0.4 percent relative to baseline, while a faster AI-driven surge could lift global growth by about 0.3 percent in 2026-27 if productivity gains arrive sooner. That asymmetry, a modest win if AI delivers against a modest loss if it doesn't, is itself the story. It is not a coin flip with equal stakes on both sides. What should worry StartupFortune's readers specifically is the private side of this. Many of the AI firms taking hyperscaler money and debt are not publicly listed, which means they report less, and a funding shortfall there doesn't show up on anyone's stock ticker until a hyperscaler writes it down. The IMF also flagged signs of rising defaults in private credit more broadly, warning they could cascade into concerns about corporate credit for highly leveraged borrowers facing AI-driven disruption to their own businesses, not just AI firms themselves. None of this means the banking system is about to seize up the way it did in 2008. The IMF's stress tests still showed banks' capital buffers remaining broadly resilient in a hypothetical downturn triggered by an AI slowdown and bond-market fragility. But the Fund's own numbers show the cushion thinning, not thickening, year over year. A fifth of global banking assets now sit in institutions the IMF classifies as weak under stress. That is the kind of detail that does not make headlines the way a stock crash does, and it is exactly the kind of detail that matters more.

results.title: IMF Warns AI Market Correction Could Trigger Global Financial Turmoil – Unite.AI
highlights: The International Monetary Fund released its October 2026 Global Financial Stability Report on October 13, 2026, warning that weaker or less durable investment and profitability in artificial intelligence could trigger a correction in AI-linked equities and credit, one of three salient risks it says could abruptly tighten financial conditions worldwide. The report, titled Resilience, Risk, and Transformation, finds that financial markets have remained resilient on solid economic growth and strong corporate earnings while financial stability risks stay elevated. Its opening chapter names an AI-driven market correction, a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields, and cyber threats as plausible near-term catalysts for market turmoil. The chapter notes that 14 of 33 major central banks have raised policy rates since the second quarter of 2026, up from two in the first quarter, in response to inflationary pressure from the Middle East energy shock. Writing in an accompanying IMF blog post, Athanasios Vamvakidis and Jason Wu wrote that there is “no room for complacency.” The report states that faltering AI investment and profitability could challenge optimistic expectations, citing growing evidence that AI capabilities can be delivered at lower investment levels or that economic gains may be smaller than expected. It points to a World Economic Outlook scenario in which an unwinding of AI investment reduces global GDP, investment, and consumption by as much as 0.4, 1.3, and 0.6 percent, respectively, by 2028. Circular financing arrangements reinforce these interdependencies. Fourteen publicly disclosed transactions since 2023 account for approximately $300 billion of equity investments led by hyperscalers in financially weaker AI firms, supplemented by $650 billion in debt, in exchange for $1.4 trillion in future revenue commitments through services or chip orders. About $320 billion of the debt sits with investees, including debt backed by investor guarantees, contingent financing, and other off-balance-sheet obligations. The report’s first chapter, “Beneath the Resilience: Rising Risks, Unresolved Vulnerabilities,” warns that distress at key investee firms could present significant “wrong-way risk”: the equity and debt investments lose value at the same time the revenue streams tied to them are impaired. The consequences of a correction could be global, the report finds. Advanced Asian equity markets show the highest sensitivity to global AI equity returns, while the euro area and the United Kingdom show low sensitivity, though stress could still transmit through sharply increased holdings of US equities between 2022 and 2026. Global sovereign bond yields have risen on higher energy prices and rising term premiums, which now sit at the upper end of their historical ranges, and the report assesses bond market risks as having worsened since the April 2026 edition. Because government bonds underpin the financial system, a sharp rise in yields would depress valuations across other assets through higher discount rates, including AI-related holdings, and erode the value of bonds used as collateral. The IMF’s 2026 Global Bank Stress Test models an adverse scenario combining weaker-than-expected AI productivity gains with short- and long-term bond yield increases of 150 and 300 basis points, cutting global real GDP growth about 3 percentage points below baseline in the first two years and raising unemployment 3.5 percentage points. Under that scenario, the global banking system’s aggregate Common Equity Tier 1 ratio falls about 150 basis points to roughly 11.5 percent, remaining well above regulatory minimums. Banks representing 22 percent of global banking assets are nonetheless classified as weak, with post-stress ratios below 7 percent, up from 18 percent in the 2025 exercise. Vulnerabilities outside banking could amplify stress. In the United States, bank loans to nonbank financial intermediaries rose 18 percent in 2026 while exposures to private equity and private credit firms rose 30 percent. Pension funds and insurers have nearly doubled their share of illiquid investments over the past decade and hold more than one-quarter of publicly traded corporate bonds in the United States and the euro area. Direct lending now accounts for nearly $2 trillion globally, and four of 10 large business development companies reviewed carry liquidity commitments exceeding their available buffers. The report urges policymakers to contain excessive leverage financing the AI ecosystem, including restrictions on equity margin financing, limits on leveraged exchange-traded funds, and containment of short-term options, backed by sectoral capital requirements, concentration limits, and capital buffers where vulnerabilities are material. On bond markets, it calls for credible fiscal consolidation, greater central clearing of bonds and repurchase agreements, and central bank liquidity facilities that are operationally ready. On cyber, the report recommends a systemwide operational resilience framework tailored to each economy’s cyber maturity, cautioning that AI compresses the attack–defense cycle to machine speed. The blog distills three priorities: put public debt on a sustainable path, limit leverage and liquidity mismatches in AI, private credit, and other nonbank financial sectors, and strengthen cyber defenses, with emerging and developing economies advised to rebuild buffers while financial conditions remain accommodative.
