results.title: World Economic Outlook, October 2026; Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices; October 13, 2026
highlights: However, this resilience is under strain. Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing pol icy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience. Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions. Other commodity markets also face risks. Low-income countries and households remain especially vulnera ble to higher food prices from transport disruptions, higher fertilizer costs, export restrictions, and extreme weather events. Technology-related investment, while an important boon against the energy shock, is concentrating risks: With gains clustered in a small number of firms, sectors, and economies, global expan sion is heavily reliant on a narrow set of technological and financial conditions. More generally, resilience has been uneven, varying noticeably with economies’ exposure to the war and the AI boom, and causing divergent outcomes. Policy constraints are also more binding now. Borrowing costs have risen sharply in major advanced economies, owing to both supply- and demand-driven price pressures, along with fiscal and credit risks. Pub lic debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from aging populations, climate change, and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks. The interaction of higher financing costs with elevated debt levels exposes a key margin of vulnerability. Strong and deliberate actions are required to rebuild buffers and shore up the capac ity to withstand future shocks—new or the same. Fiscal policy must be restrained and help contain demand pressures at a time of heightened inflationary risks. While monetary policy tightened significantly in the aftermath of the pandemic, primary deficits have remained elevated and are significantly larger than before the pandemic in many countries. Importantly, the increase in borrowing costs and its implications for fiscal sustainability make the need for fiscal adjustment all the more urgent. Chapter 1 of this report considers a risk scenario in which there is a loss of fiscal and monetary credibility in major economies, in addition 2026 to commodity price increases. In that scenario, global growth in 2027 would be materially lower than in the baseline projections, with inflation significantly higher; the shock would have tangible spillovers for emerging market and developing economies. To prevent such a scenario, public debt levels need to be put back on a durably sustainable path. Chapter 2 underscores that, in cost-of-living crises, measures that preserve price signals and rely primarily on temporary and targeted income support for the most vulnerable households are both effective and efficient. Chapter 3 shows that corporate income tax policy can help from the revenue side but has important domestic and cross-border implications: Debt-financed tax cuts may support activity in the short term but can crowd out invest ment elsewhere, while the reduction in tax revenues can constrain public investment and productive capac ity over time. In turn, monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability, in line with central banks’ mandates. The policy stance should be sufficiently restrictive to return inflation to target in a timely fashion, preventing second-round effects. Where com modity price increases and technology-related invest ment (or other factors) add to persistent inflationary pressures, monetary policy will need to tighten further. Starting levels of inflation, labor market tightness, and technology and commodity exposures remain key pol icy guideposts. The appropriate stance will differ across countries, but the objective is the same: to ensure price stability. Central bank independence is instrumental in achieving that goal. Over the medium term, a comprehensive strategy to guarantee supply-side resilience is essential in an environment marked by virulent weather events and heightened geopolitically induced disruptions. Such a strategy should rest on three mutually reinforc ing pillars. The first is technological diversification: greater investment in critical technologies and inputs for which substitutes are limited. Energy is a clear example. Diversification means continuing to expand sources of energy, including renewables. Progress is already underway, with clean energy generation rising rapidly. But the transition must go further. The second pillar is trade diversification. More diversified trade relationships reduce exposure to individual input sup pliers and buyers and can lower volatility. Reshoring is not a viable solution for most countries; it is often inefficient and can increase the concentration of risks in the domestic economy. The third pillar, comple menting the previous two, is stronger supply buffers in critical sectors, such as energy, water, food, and other essential inputs. A Fiscal vulnerabilities and renewed trade tensions could further weaken growth. Upside risks are also evident: AI-related investment could prove more persistent, productivity gains could materialize faster than assumed, new trade arrangements could improve pre dictability and resilience, and higher fossil fuel prices could accelerate investment in energy security. Policy needs to navigate competing forces without losing sight of medium-term stability. Given elevated debt, rising sovereign yields, and pressing spending needs, a renewed focus on rebuilding fiscal space is increasingly urgent. Governments should imple ment credible fiscal adjustment plans that combine enhancements on the revenue side with spending rationalization, supported by institutional improve ments. Any support to ease the impact of higher energy and food prices should be temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary, and should not jeopardize fiscal sustainability goals. Monetary policy needs to be tailored to circumstances, in line with central banks’ mandates, considering initial conditions before the war, inflation expectations and broader underlying inflation gauges, and the level of the policy rate relative to its neutral level. The case for maintaining a cautious stance is strongest in energy importers outside the technology value chain with inflation at or below target, while the case for tightening is strongest in economies that are plugged into stronger demand pressures from the technology value chain, where inflation was already above target before the twin shocks and remains so, and where broader price pressures are expected to remain elevated. At a struc tural level, strengthening energy security, improving AI readiness, and maintaining open channels for trade and cooperation are essential to raising resilience in a world where shocks are increasingly frequent and asymmetric. The analytical chapters of this report provide insights on fiscal frameworks that could deliver better results when dealing with disruptive shocks and building policy space through revenue measures. As Chapter 2 demonstrates, when faced with cost of-living crises, governments should preserve price sig nals and rely primarily on temporary, targeted income support for the most vulnerable, underscoring the importance of investing in stronger social protection systems that can be rapidly scaled up during crises. As Chapter 3 shows, the global effects of changes in corporate income tax (CIT) policy depend on how governments’ budgets adjust: Debt-financed tax cuts support domestic activity but can crowd out invest ment in other economies and generate negative spill overs in the short term. In the long term, spillovers can be positive, owing to cross-border knowledge trans fers, while presenting trade-offs domestically if lower revenues constrain public investment and productive capacity, notably for emerging market and developing economies, which rely more heavily on CIT revenues.

results.title: IMF: BOJ to Keep Raising Rates Even as Japan's Growth Slows — Daily Digest Invest
highlights: - The IMF sees Japan's economy growing just 0.7% in 2026 and 2027, yet expects the Bank of Japan to keep raising rates gradually. - It also notes room for intervention if yen swings turn disorderly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released its latest World Economic Outlook, and for Japan, the picture is one of slow growth but continued monetary tightening. The IMF projects Japan's economy will expand by just 0.7% in both 2026 and 2027, a modest pace that reflects an aging population and subdued productivity gains. Despite that sluggish backdrop, the IMF expects the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to keep nudging interest rates higher, moving gradually toward what it calls a “neutral” rate—a level that neither stimulates nor restricts economic activity. The BOJ has already lifted its policy rate to 1.25%, the highest in 31 years, in September. That move came after years of ultra-loose monetary policy aimed at fighting deflation. Now, with inflation running above the central bank's 2% target, the BOJ is shifting gears. The IMF's view is that the BOJ will continue this gradual tightening cycle, even as growth slows, because the risk of entrenched inflation outweighs the drag on the economy. This is a delicate balancing act. On one hand, higher rates could cool an already weak economy. On the other, leaving rates too low for too long could allow inflation to become embedded in wages and prices, which would be harder to reverse. The IMF's assessment suggests it believes the BOJ will prioritize price stability, accepting slower growth as the cost of normalizing policy. For investors, this means Japanese government bond yields could keep drifting higher, and the yen may find some support from the rate differential with other major economies, though that support could be limited if global growth also slows. The bond market is already split on whether another hike is coming, and the IMF's outlook adds weight to the hawks' case. The broader context is that the IMF's global growth forecast for 2026 was nudged up to 3.1%, but it also flagged risks, including trade tensions and geopolitical shocks. Japan's slow growth is part of a wider pattern of moderate expansion in advanced economies, with France's economy stalling and other nations facing similar headwinds. For investors with exposure to Japan, the key takeaway is that the BOJ is likely to keep tightening, which has several implications. First, Japanese government bonds may offer higher yields, making them more attractive relative to other developed-market bonds. Second, the yen could strengthen if the BOJ continues to hike while other central banks, like the Federal Reserve, are cutting or pausing. That would affect returns for foreign investors in Japanese stocks, as a stronger yen can reduce the value of their holdings when converted back to their home currency. For now, the message is clear: Japan is in a slow-growth, gradual-tightening regime. Investors should expect more rate hikes, potential currency intervention, and a bond market that may remain volatile. As always, diversification and a long-term perspective are key, especially when navigating a market that is undergoing a historic policy shift.

results.title: IMF Urges Caution on BoJ Rate Hikes
highlights: The Bank of Japan should maintain its loose monetary policy and raise interest rates only gradually amid persistent global trade uncertainties, said Deputy Director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department Nada Choueiri. She noted that Japan’s economy has exceeded expectations this year, helped by solid consumption and exports, while a trade deal with the U.S. has eased some of the uncertainty. However, risks remain tilted to the downside due to unresolved U.S.-China trade tensions and potential shifts in global conditions. “Going forward, gradualism is very important because of the degree of uncertainty,” Choueiri told Reuters, stressing the need to monitor incoming data closely. Bank of Japan policy board member Hajime Takata renewed his call for an interest rate hike, citing eased tariff concerns and progress toward the central bank’s inflation target. “Headline inflation has stayed at 2% or above for three and a half years,” he said in a speech on Monday, adding that “now is a prime opportunity to raise the policy interest rate.” Takata had previously proposed lifting the rate to 0.75% from 0.5%, a motion rejected in September. He argued that Japan’s economy is nearing the price stability goal, increasing the likelihood he will push for a hike at the October 29–30 meeting. Takata also downplayed risks of a U.S. downturn, pointing to solid household, corporate, and financial sector balance sheets. He noted the Fed’s September rate cut did not trigger an unwanted yen appreciation, and that U.S. tariffs have not discouraged Japanese firms from investing in equipment and wages. Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said Thursday the central bank will closely examine a range of data—including insights gathered during his Washington visit—before deciding whether to raise interest rates in October. He reiterated that a rate hike will depend on whether the probability of meeting the bank’s growth and inflation forecasts increases. Speaking after the G7 and G20 finance meetings, Ueda noted that while global and U.S. economies remain resilient, the effects of U.S. tariffs are expected to surface soon. On the domestic front, Japan’s two major political parties, the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and the Constitutional Democratic Party (CDP), have reached a broad agreement to hold a parliamentary vote on October 21 to select the next prime minister, according to Kyodo News.

results.title: ‘Clear and present danger’: fuel prices could rise by 30c a litre across Australia under IMF scenario | 24NewsDesk
highlights: Outlook shows how a worsening Middle East crisis could could rise by c a litre An International Monetary Fund scenario where global oil prices jump to $US130 a barrel over coming months could push Australian petrol prices up by another 30 cents and pile pressure on the Reserve Bank to hike interest rates, economists say. In its latest World Economic Outlook, the IMF modelled the impact on global growth and inflation from a worsening Middle East crisis that extended into next year, highlighting the “clear and present danger” to a resilient global economy from turmoil in commodity and bond markets. The IMF described a scenario where “the conflict persists through the end of June 2027, keeping the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb largely closed to commercial shipping, extending damages to oil infrastructures in the region, and delaying the recovery in oil supply to the end of 2027”. “With limited scope for further inventory drawdown, oil prices reach $US130 from the fourth quarter of 2026 to the first quarter of 2027.” Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said “the reality” was that the RBA – alongside other central banks – would have to respond to higher fuel costs with higher interest rates. The RBA delivered a fourth interest rate hike last month. Minutes from that meeting released on Tuesday showed that board members discussed how “the Middle East conflict had escalated and oil prices were substantially above the level assumed in the August forecasts”. Should global oil prices instead push towards $US1.30, as per the IMF scenario (and assuming each $US10 oil price increase leads to a 10c rise in fuel prices), inflation could instead still be as high as 4.5% in late 2026. But McMenamin was less convinced the RBA would have to respond with higher interest rates, saying the central bank has been mostly responding to underlying price pressures related to domestic capacity constraints, rather than overseas factors.

results.title: World Economic Outlook, October 2026; Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices; October 13, 2026
highlights: : With gains clustered in a small number of firms, sectors, and economies, global expan sion is heavily reliant on a narrow set of technological and financial conditions. More generally, resilience has been uneven, varying noticeably with economies’ exposure to the war and the AI boom, and causing divergent outcomes. Policy constraints are also more binding now. Borrowing costs have risen sharply in major advanced economies, owing to both supply- and demand-driven price pressures, along with fiscal and credit risks. Pub lic debt is high in many economies, WORLD ECONOMIC OUTLOOK: Resilience Under Strain, Urgent Choices xii International Monetary Fund | October 2026 to commodity price increases. In that scenario, global growth in 2027 would be materially lower than in the baseline projections, with inflation significantly higher; the shock would have tangible spillovers for emerging market and developing economies. To prevent such a scenario, public debt levels need to be put back on a durably sustainable path. Chapter 2 underscores that, in cost-of-living crises, measures that preserve price signals and rely primarily on temporary and targeted income support for the most vulnerable households are both effective and efficient. Chapter 3 shows that corporate income tax policy can help from the revenue side but has important domestic and cross-border implications: Debt-financed tax cuts may support activity in the short term but can crowd out invest ment elsewhere, while the reduction in tax revenues can constrain public investment and productive capac ity over time. In turn, monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability, in line with central banks’ mandates. The policy stance should be sufficiently restrictive to return inflation to target in a timely fashion, preventing second-round effects. Where com modity price increases and technology-related invest ment (or other factors) add to persistent inflationary pressures, monetary policy will need to tighten further. Starting levels of inflation, labor market tightness, and technology and commodity exposures remain key pol icy guideposts. The appropriate stance will differ across countries, but the objective is the same: to ensure price stability. Central bank independence is instrumental in achieving that goal. Over the medium term, a comprehensive strategy to guarantee supply-side resilience is essential in an environment marked by virulent weather events and heightened geopolitically induced disruptions. Such a strategy should rest on three mutually reinforc ing pillars. The first is technological diversification: greater investment in critical technologies and inputs for which substitutes are limited. Energy is a clear example. Diversification means continuing to expand sources of energy, including renewables. Progress is already underway, with clean energy generation rising rapidly. But the transition must go further. The second pillar is trade diversification. More diversified trade relationships reduce exposure to individual input sup pliers and buyers and can lower volatility. Reshoring is not a viable solution for most countries; it is often inefficient and can increase the concentration of risks in the domestic economy. The third pillar, comple menting the previous two, is stronger supply buffers in critical sectors, such as energy, water, food, and other essential inputs. A well-designed strategy must encom pass both the public and private sectors, with the latter bolstered by structural reforms to boost entrepreneur ship and business dynamism. Its objective should be not only to help economies cope with shocks ex post, but also to reduce exposure ex ante; limit abrupt and costly adjustments; and strengthen economies’ ability to grow. Last but not least, international cooperation remains indispensable. Many of the shocks weighing on the global economy cross borders, and so must the response. In a more shock-prone and still intercon nected world, resilience cannot be built by countries acting alone. Transparent and predictable trade rules can facilitate long-term planning and enhance invest ment. Cooperation on energy security and critical sup ply chains can make adjustment less disruptive when shocks occur. As artificial intelligence reshapes produc tion and trade, policymakers must work together to prudently harness and broaden the gains and manage the risks from technological transformation. The ben efits of innovation should help raise living standards and make growth more durable and inclusive. The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuild ing: rebuilding supply-side resilience, restoring fiscal space, lifting growth potential, and ensuring that the next decade is defined by growth and shared prosperity. This issue of the World Economic Outlook was made possible by the hard work and dedication of the staff in the IMF research and area departments, and the vision and thoughtful guidance of my predecessor, Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas. Fiscal vulnerabilities and renewed trade tensions could further weaken growth. Upside risks are also evident: AI-related investment could prove more persistent, productivity gains could materialize faster than assumed, new trade arrangements could improve pre dictability and resilience, and higher fossil fuel prices could accelerate investment in energy security. Policy needs to navigate competing forces without losing sight of medium-term stability. Given elevated debt, rising sovereign yields, and pressing spending needs, a renewed focus on rebuilding fiscal space is increasingly urgent. Governments should imple ment credible fiscal adjustment plans that combine enhancements on the revenue side with spending rationalization, supported by institutional improve ments. Any support to ease the impact of higher energy and food prices should be temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary, and should not jeopardize fiscal sustainability goals. Monetary policy needs to be tailored to circumstances, in line with central banks’ mandates, considering initial conditions before the war, inflation expectations and broader underlying inflation gauges, and the level of the policy rate relative to its neutral level. The case for maintaining a cautious stance is strongest in energy importers outside the technology value chain with inflation at or below target, while the case for tightening is strongest in economies that are plugged into stronger demand pressures from the technology value chain, where inflation was already above target before the twin shocks and remains so, and where broader price pressures are expected to remain elevated. At a struc tural level, strengthening energy security, improving AI readiness, and maintaining open channels for trade and cooperation are essential to raising resilience in a world where shocks are increasingly frequent and asymmetric. The analytical chapters of this report provide insights on fiscal frameworks that could deliver better results when dealing with disruptive shocks and building policy space through revenue measures. As Chapter 2 demonstrates, when faced with cost of-living crises, governments should preserve price sig nals and rely primarily on temporary, targeted income support for the most vulnerable, underscoring the importance of investing in stronger social protection systems that can be rapidly scaled up during crises. As Chapter 3 shows, the global effects of changes in corporate income tax (CIT) policy depend on how governments’ budgets adjust: Debt-financed tax cuts support domestic activity but can crowd out invest ment in other economies and generate negative spill overs in the short term. In the long term, spillovers can be positive, owing to cross-border knowledge trans fers, while presenting trade-offs domestically if lower revenues constrain public investment and productive capacity, notably for emerging market and developing economies, which rely more heavily on CIT revenues.

highlights: Disclaimer: The World Economic Outlook (WEO) is a survey by the IMF staff pub lished twice a year, in spring and fall. The WEO is prepared by the IMF staff and has benefited from comments and suggestions by Executive Directors following their discussion of the report on September 28, 2026. In less than seven years, the global economy has been subjected to an exceptional sequence of events. The pandemic and the ensuing disruptions to global supply chains; the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, with the consequent sharp increases in the prices of energy and other commodities; and significant changes in trade barriers and trading relations have tested the resilience of households, firms, financial markets, and governments. Individually, each of these major developments would have been considered unlikely. Their confluence over such a short period of time is even more extraordinary. Yet, despite this barrage of shocks, the global economy has held up. Labor markets have remained unexpectedly strong; financial systems have broadly withstood the shocks and the sharpest monetary tightening in half a century; and inflation has receded from its peaks in many economies, although it remains persistent in some cases. This resilience is reflected in our latest global growth forecast, which remains broadly unchanged from April, despite a more persistent energy market disruption than anticipated. Global activity is projected to grow at 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027. Global headline inflation is projected to rise to 4.7 percent this year, reflecting primarily higher commodity prices, and to fall back to 4.1 percent in 2027; the pass through to core inflation is expected to be limited. What has helped the global economy withstand this latest shock? There are two main sets of factors. First, the rerouting of energy supplies; increased energy production in other countries; inventory drawdowns; substitution to other sources of energy, including renewables; and higher energy efficiency have all helped cushion the impact on energy markets. Without these margins of adjustment, the oil disrup tion alone would have significantly reduced global growth in 2026. Second, the investment boom triggered by artificial intelligence has provided impetus to global activity and supported international trade. Investment has contin ued to rise in anticipation of higher expected returns and real incomes (reflected in stock valuations). | October 2 The global economy is again proving resilient, but unevenly so and with rapidly narrowing margins of adjustment in the near term. Activity in the first half of 2026 held up better than expected despite the drag ging war in the Middle East and continuing strains from trade tensions. The technology cycle has pro vided a demand impulse, driven by strong investment in artificial intelligence (AI). The interaction of these forces—geopolitics and technology—has produced a split global economy: Favorable terms of trade or technology-related exports and investment give some countries a cushion, whereas others face higher import bills and weaker demand. Use of buffers and adaptabil ity have helped economies weather the negative shocks so far. Flexible supply responses, rerouting of ship ments, inventory drawdowns, fiscal support measures, and lower energy intensity than in previous decades have helped contain the hit to activity from the war. Private firms have continued to adjust to repeated shocks, including geopolitical risk and shifts in trade policy, while financial markets have maintained a broadly benign view of the challenges, also buoyed by exuberance in the technology segment. Yet these margins of adjustment are not unlimited. Inventories have been drawn down, commodity markets remain vulnerable, fragmentation could become a greater drag on efficiency, prolonged uncertainty could eventually weigh more heavily on confidence, constraints on energy could impair the AI-led impetus, and financing conditions could change abruptly for any number of reasons, including fiscal sustainability concerns. Global growth is projected at 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, unchanged for 2026 and revised moderately upward for 2027, relative to the projections in the April 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO). Global headline inflation is projected to increase to 4.7 percent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 percent in 2027, marking a cumulative upward revision of 0.7 percentage point with the temporary increase driven mainly by energy and food prices. The stable global aggregate masks a reallocation of growth across economies. Countries with limited direct exposure to the war shock and strong participation in the technology upturn are seeing activity hold up or strengthen. Energy exporters outside the immediate conflict zone benefit from favorable terms of trade. Conversely, energy-importing economies with little connection to the technology value chain face the most difficult configuration: higher import costs and exchange rate pressures, weaker real incomes, more constrained fiscal space, and fewer offsetting demand impulses. Many low-income and vulnerable coun tries belong to this latter group, increasing the risk that recent shocks will widen income gaps across and within countries. World trade volume growth is projected to slow in 2026 and stabilize in 2027, reflecting the drag from tariffs, adjustment in production chains, and continued strength in technology-related trade. Global imbalances are expected to decline only modestly over the medium term, as large fiscal deficits, limited domestic rebal ancing, technology-driven capital flows, and differing demand compositions across major economies under current policies continue to sustain external gaps. The medium-term growth outlook remains lackluster by historical standards and uneven across countries, in part reflecting varying degrees of AI preparedness and robustness of the energy mix. Risks are skewed to the downside. A prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East could keep energy and food prices elevated and volatile, revive inflationary pressures, worsen fiscal and external balances, and weigh on growth. Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyberattacks, or extreme weather events could amplify these effects. As the Commodity Special Feature shows, price increases driven by physical supply disruptions have larger and more persistent macroeconomic effects than those driven by geopolitical risks. A reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity pros pects could sharply reduce investment, trigger equity market corrections, and tighten financial conditions, with spillovers to economies integrated into technol ogy supply chains and stakes in technology stocks.

results.title: October 14 CPI: The Print That Decides the December Hike
highlights: What is not settled is December. Polymarket has a December 25-basis-point hike at 74%. Between now and the December 8-9 meeting, two major rounds of data will shape the Committee's thinking — and the most important one lands in eleven days: September CPI, released October 14 at 8:30 AM ET. That single print is now the center of gravity for the entire back half of the rate cycle. The key distinction the market is drawing: Friday's data did not end the hiking cycle. It postponed it. Average hourly earnings at 3.0% year-over-year remain above any pace consistent with 2% inflation. The three-month average for payroll additions has collapsed to roughly 50,000 — weak, but not the kind of labor market deterioration that historically pulls the Fed off a tightening bias. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said officials may need more time before deciding on another hike. New York Fed President John Williams used nearly identical language the prior week. Neither signaled a pause beyond October. The consensus read: October skips, December decides. Gasoline is the decisive variable. In August, motor fuel contributed nearly 100 basis points to the headline CPI figure on its own, running more than 34% year-over-year as Iran war supply disruptions kept oil prices elevated. September saw gasoline surge roughly 8% on the month — which would once again make energy the single largest driver of any headline acceleration. At the same time, shelter inflation decelerated to 3.0% in August from 3.2% in July, and Zillow's September forecast calls for continued rent cooling through year-end. Core CPI is widely expected near 0.2% to 0.3% month-over-month — Street consensus at 0.3%, Nowflation at 0.25%, Cleveland Fed at 0.20%. The divergence between a hot headline and a softer core is the defining setup for this release. The October 14 print resolves into three distinct probability buckets for the December hike trade, and Kalshi and Polymarket contracts will price each scenario in near real time. Scenario one — a hot print at 3.7% or above, core at 0.3% month-over-month: This outcome solidifies December. A result that matches or beats the Street on both headline and core confirms the Iran war energy shock is still feeding broadly into prices, validates hawkish Fed members who argue the job is not done, and pushes December hike odds above 80% on both platforms. Polymarket's current 74% has clear room to firm. Scenario two — an inline or soft read in the 3.5% to 3.6% range, core at 0.2%: This is the consensus case, and it likely keeps December near current pricing — 70% to 74%. The Committee reads it as confirmation that the base effect is starting to work, energy is the driver not services, and the October pause was the right call. This scenario produces the least movement in prediction market odds. December treads water until November data arrives. Scenario three — a downside surprise below 3.5%, especially if core prints 0.1%: This scenario opens the door to a year-end pause. December hike odds could fall below 60% in this case. The conditions required: shelter inflation has to continue softening meaningfully, and energy has to disappoint relative to current elevated forecasts — possible if the G7's coordinated emergency fuel release of 100 million barrels announced Friday works faster than most timelines suggest. This is the tail scenario prediction markets are not pricing today, but it is the outcome that would materially reset 2027 rate-cut expectations. Kalshi's dedicated September CPI contracts are instructive. The platform prices above 3.1% at near-certainty and above 3.0% at 99%. On Polymarket, the monthly CPI market has 0.6% at 44% and 0.5% at 35% — the crowd is betting on a hot headline print driven by energy, with meaningful uncertainty about whether the final rounding lands at 0.5% or 0.6%. That split reflects the forecaster disagreement almost exactly. A notable core CPI contract on Kalshi shows above 0.1% at 74%, meaning traders are not ruling out a very soft core number — the scenario that would allow the Fed to dismiss the headline as energy noise and hold steady through year-end. With October hold settled and December at 74%, the window for the next real move in the rate cycle has narrowed to eleven days and one data point. The October 14 print does not just decide the December trade. It sets the table for how the hiking cycle ends — or whether it continues into 2027.

results.title: Fed January 2027 Rate Hike Odds After September 2026 | Prediction.com
highlights: Fed's 027 Hike at 48% repriced January 202 by 14 percentage points in now price a near coin-flip 20 7, up from 33% three September's first hike since Prediction markets now put the probability of a Hike 25bps at the Fed decision in Jan 2027 at 48%, up from 33% three days ago, after the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate on September 16, 2026, lifting the target range by 25 basis points to 3.75-4.00%. It was the first hike since July 2023. That single decision broke a three-year pause in tightening and forced prediction markets to reprice the entire forward path for rates. The Hike 25bps outcome for the January 2027 Fed decision trades at 48% on Kalshi and 47% on Polymarket, up from 33% just three days ago. That 14-percentage-point swing, off a period low of 32%, reflects a market that went from treating further tightening as a tail risk to pricing it as nearly a coin flip. The speed of the move matters as much as the level: this was not a gradual drift driven by ambiguous data. It was a step-function repricing triggered by a concrete policy action. The proof point that makes this repricing hard to dismiss is the updated dot plot. The Fed's Summary of Economic Projections now shows the median funds rate holding at 4.1% through the end of 2027. That projection leaves no room for cuts. More critically, it leaves a credible path to another hike: if inflation data between now and January comes in hot, 4.1% becomes a floor, not a ceiling. The hike was driven by what the Fed cited as persistent inflation and stronger-than-expected economic conditions. The combination justifies continued tightening: an economy running hot enough to sustain demand-driven price pressures even at already-elevated rates. The Dow fell 631 points on the day of the decision, a measure of how thoroughly the market had positioned for a different outcome. What moved the January 2027 market from 33% to 48% was not just the September hike itself. It was the dot plot's message that 4.1% represents the committee's median expectation for the funds rate through all of 2027. That projection, combined with the demonstrated willingness to hike after a three-year pause, eliminates the asymmetry that had kept hike probabilities low. Before September, betting on a hike required believing the Fed would restart a dormant cycle. That barrier no longer exists. The cycle is restarted. The question is only whether the next data prints justify extending it. Two FOMC meetings stand between 27 resolution: October 28 and December 9, according the published schedule. Each meeting gives Fed an opportunity hike, hold, or signal its January intentions through forward guidance. If the Fed holds at both October and December, a January hike would represent a measured, every-other-meeting pace. If it hikes again before January, the 48% implied probability for consecutive January hike may actually under the risk. A 48% probability means the market assigns a 52% chance that the Fed does something other than hike 25bps in January. That "something else" is overwhelmingly a hold. The strongest case against a January hike rests on three pillars, each worth serious consideration. First, inflation could decelerate between now and late January. The September hike was motivated by insufficient progress on prices. If the October and November CPI readings show meaningful disinflation, the Fed's own framework would argue against tightening further. The dot plot is a projection, not a promise. It shifts with data. Third, the Fed may simply prefer to wait. The September hike was the first in three years. Policymakers may want to observe its effects on financial conditions, credit markets, and housing before moving again. A three-meeting gap (September to January, skipping October and December) would be consistent with a cautious, data-dependent posture. Any Fed Chair language emphasizing patience or watching the data would likely push the 48% figure back down. With four months and two FOMC meetings still ahead, every major data release between now and January 27 has the potential to move this market by another double-digit swing. The 48% Hike 25bps price is the headline, but the full distribution tells a richer story about how much uncertainty the September hike injected into the rate path.

results.title: Four reasons behind our higher Fed interest rate forecast
highlights: - Martin Hochstein 25/09/2026 We now expect the US Federal Reserve (Fed) to raise rates by a further 75 basis points by the second quarter of 2027, taking the federal funds target range to 4.5-4.75%. This is 50 basis points higher than our previous forecast. We continue to expect one additional 25 basis points increase by the end of 2026. Our revised view follows the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) September meeting, at which it raised the federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75-4.0%. The Fed is no longer giving forward guidance, creating uncertainty about the timing and magnitude of future moves. Even so, recent comments from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh point to further tightening, and we see four developments supporting a higher terminal rate. The hawkish tilt is reflected in the FOMC’s dot plot. The median policymaker expects one further 25 basis points hike this year and no additional move in 2027. However, four participants expect two further hikes in 2026, while eight anticipate a total of 50 basis points of further tightening by the end of 2027. The median long-run dot – an indication of the FOMC’s estimate of the longerterm neutral rate – has risen to 3.25%. But inflation remains elevated and has been above target for more than five years. Mr Warsh stressed that the underlying trend had not improved meaningfully and remained too broadbased. Rising commodity prices add another upside risk. The FOMC’s September economic projections highlight the tension. The median projection is for real GDP growth of 2.3% this year and 2.4% next year, with unemployment holding at 4.1% throughout the forecast horizon. However, inflation is expected to decline only gradually. Core personal consumption expenditures (PCE) inflation is expected to ease from 3.4% this year to 2.5% next year and 2.2% in 2028, before reaching the 2% target only in 2029. 1 In our view, the no-landing economic backdrop makes the inflation outlook harder to call. With growth above potential and employment still strong, inflation is unlikely to return sustainably to target without some cooling in the economy. Structural pressures compound that challenge. Mr Warsh has argued that lower inflation does not need to mean weaker employment, but we think that trade-off will become harder to avoid as policy tightens. At Jackson Hole, Mr Warsh said underlying inflation needed to move towards the 2% target clearly and at sufficient speed. In September, he judged that this test had not been passed. The rate hike was presented as a necessary step to reduce support for the economy and help inflation return to target sooner, rather than as a technical response to a higher neutral rate or a symbolic move to bolster credibility. The Fed has begun to take support out of the economy, moving policy to a tighter stance. The September increase is likely to be the first step in a longer cycle rather than a one-off move. Financial conditions still support growth, the economy remains resilient, and inflation is the Fed’s main concern. The need to reinforce its commitment to price stability also points to further rate rises. 1 Source: Summary of Economic Projections, US Federal Reserve, 16 September 2026. Investing involves risk. results.title: Markets Price More Fed Rate Hikes Into 2027
highlights: Markets are now pricing in more Fed rate hikes. After the Federal Reserve lifted its target range to 3.75% to 4.00% in September, markets expect the policy rate to approach 4.7% by mid-2027. This week’s feature puts that shift next to the rest of the recent data. You’ll see August industrial production, which stalled as manufacturing output fell and snapped seven straight monthly gains, along with a jump in new home sales and initial jobless claims of 197,000. On the market side, stocks reached a record 48% of US household assets in June, and consensus earnings estimates for 2026 and 2027 have kept moving higher. The article also shows how GDP growth has behaved in past Fed tightening cycles, split between those followed by soft landings and those followed by recessions. Following last week’s 25-basis-point rate hike that lifted the federal funds target range to 3.75%–4.00%, markets are pricing in further tightening, with the policy rate expected to approach 4.7% by mid-2027. How markets react to the tightening depends on how economic conditions unfold. To put the current cycle in context, the charts below divide Fed tightening episodes since the mid-1960s into two groups: those followed by soft landings and those followed by recessions. Inflation pressures are being driven by three largely temporary supply shocks—tariffs, energy, and the AI buildout—with tariff pass-through already past its peak and the other pressures expected to ease in 2027, according to Alpine Macro.

This page translates that pricing into a readable meeting-by-meeting rate path using the step size selected. Use it as a pricing dashboard—not a forecast—to monitor expectations. | Meeting | Implied Rate(Post-Meeting) | Probability of Hike(Cut) | # of Hikes(Cuts) | Δ vs Current (bps) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Jan 28, 2026 | 3.60% | (18.0%) | (0.18) | -4.5 | | Mar 18, 2026 | 3.50% | (38.0%) | (0.56) | -14.0 | | Apr 29, 2026 | 3.43% | (28.0%) | (0.84) | -21.0 | | Jun 17, 2026 | 3.29% | (55.2%) | (1.39) | -34.8 | | Jul 29, 2026 | 3.22% | (28.8%) | (1.68) | -42.0 | | Sep 16, 2026 | 3.13% | (34.4%) | (2.02) | -50.6 | | Oct 28, 2026 | 3.10% | (15.6%) | (2.18) | -54.5 | | Dec 9, 2026 | 3.06% | (14.0%) | (2.32) | -58.0 | 25bps hike 45.2% priced in - Implied post-meeting rate is the expected federal funds rate target band midpoint after each meeting. - Probability of hike/cut displays an approximate probability of a fed funds rate move at each meeting (step size defaults to 25bps moves but can be changed in the drop-down menu). - # of hikes/cuts shows the cumulative number of hikes/cuts expected between now and each meeting (also dependent on the step size selected). - Δ vs current (bps) shows the cumulative change in the effective fed funds midpoint priced-in between now and each meeting in basis points (+12.5bps = +0.125%). The chart plots the implied post-meeting rate across all upcoming meetings. An upward-sloping line indicates that markets are pricing further tightening over time; a flat line suggests an extended pause; a downward-sloping line indicates expected cuts. Use the screen to see what is currently priced in and to compare today’s expectations with those from previous weeks or months. What “probabilities” mean (and what they don’t) The probabilities on this site are market-implied. They describe what is priced, not what will happen. Markets can overreact, underreact, or price scenarios that never occur. The goal is to translate market pricing into a clean, intuitive summary of expectations using a consistent step size. Step size matters because markets may be pricing smaller adjustments, larger moves, or a mix of outcomes across meetings. The probability fields are therefore best read as approximations that help summarize pricing, rather than precise forecasts. In rates-market shorthand, a meeting is "live" when a policy move there is a realistic possibility, even if it isn't the most likely outcome. The liveness gauge applies this to the next scheduled meeting: it reads LIVE once the probability of a hike or cut (at your selected step size) reaches 25%, and DEAD below that. There's no official threshold for "live." We use 25%, a one-in-four chance (6.25bps priced at the default 25bps step), because that is where a move stops being a long shot: by 25%, widely used probability-language scales, such as the IPCC's and those used by US and UK intelligence analysts, no longer describe an outcome as "very" or "highly" unlikely. It is still a judgment call, which is why the exact probability is always shown in the gauge's tooltip and elsewhere. STRENGTH uses an asymmetric scale to show how firmly the meeting sits on its side of that line: STRONG under 10%, MODERATE 10–20% and WEAK 20–25% on the dead side; WEAK 25–40%, MODERATE 40–70% and STRONG 70% and above on the live side. The tooltip's Conviction score is a separate, outcome-neutral measure (the same one used on the comparison page): it is lowest at a 50/50 split and highest when pricing is near 0% or 100%. Like every probability on this site, the gauge reflects market pricing, not a forecast. See the methodology page for the full method, the reasoning behind each cutoff, and its limitations. Methodology summary At a high level, the site uses interest-rate market instruments that reference future policy settings to infer an expected policy-rate path meeting-by-meeting. Those implied levels are translated into an implied post-meeting path and a cumulative change versus current, along with approximate probabilities of discrete moves based on the selected step size. Data is updated 3x per day. If the most recent fetch is temporarily unavailable, the page may display the most recent cached values. Note: These probabilities are derived from OIS (overnight index swap) markets, not Fed funds futures contracts. These instruments are closely related and often move together, but this site's calculations are OIS-based throughout. About the Federal Reserve The Federal Reserve is the central bank of the United States. Its mandate, set by Congress in the Federal Reserve Act, is to promote maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates — commonly called the "dual mandate," since stable prices and anchored long-term rates are treated as complementary outcomes of the same inflation objective. The FOMC's longer-run inflation goal is a straightforward 2% target, measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE). The Committee's primary tool is the target range for the federal funds rate (the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to one another), supported by balance sheet policies and forward guidance. The federal funds rate isn't set directly; the Fed instead uses a set of administered rates to keep the actual traded rate inside its target range. Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB) —what the Fed pays banks on reserves held at the Fed— sits inside the range and is the primary lever nudging market rates toward target. The overnight reverse repo facility (ON RRP) rate is set at the bottom of the range, giving money market funds, government-sponsored enterprises, and other eligible counterparties a floor return that keeps rates from slipping below the band. Two facilities anchor the top of the range: the standing repo facility (SRF), where eligible institutions can borrow cash overnight against high-quality collateral, and the discount window's primary credit rate —commonly called "the discount rate"— the Fed's traditional lender-of-last-resort facility. The discount rate has been set equal to the top of the target range since March 2020, when the Fed narrowed the spread to reduce the stigma associated with discount window borrowing. Together, these tools keep the actual traded rate — the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) — within the FOMC's target range. Interest rate decisions are made by the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), which has 12 voting members: the seven-member Board of Governors, each nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate to staggered 14-year terms; the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, a permanent voter who also serves as the Committee's Vice Chair; and four of the remaining 11 Reserve Bank presidents, who rotate onto the Committee for one-year terms. The FOMC normally meets eight times per year (roughly every six weeks). At each decision point the Committee may leave the target range unchanged ("hold"), raise it ("hike"), or lower it ("cut"). In extraordinary circumstances, the FOMC can also change rates between scheduled meetings.

results.title: Fed January 2027 Hike Odds Fall After Jobs Report | Prediction.com
highlights: The probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike at its January 2027 meeting sits at 34%, down from 48% three days ago, after the September 2026 jobs report landed in a policy dead zone: too strong to worry about, too cool to act on. Unemployment fell to 4.4% with solid but unspectacular wage growth, a combination that strips the hawkish case of its central argument. If the labor market is not overheating, what exactly would the Fed be tightening against? Prediction markets answered that question with a swift repricing. The implied probability of a Hike 25bps at the January 2027 Fed decision dropped from 48% to 34% over three days, a 14-percentage-point decline that reflects a genuine shift in how traders assess the Fed's next move. The period low touched 32%, meaning the current 34% sits just above the floor. This was not a gradual drift. It was a conviction trade triggered by data that was good news for the economy but bad news for anyone positioned for tighter policy. The Fed operates under a dual mandate: price stability and maximum employment. The September report made it harder to build a case on either front. Unemployment at 4.4% is falling, not rising, which eliminates the argument that the labor market needs intervention. Wage growth remains solid but is not accelerating at a pace that would signal embedded inflationary pressure. According to MarketScreener, the data led analysts to anticipate the Fed will maintain current interest rates at its January meeting. This creates what might be called the "Goldilocks trap" for hike advocates. The economy would need to show clear signs of overheating, runaway wages, or an inflation resurgence to justify moving rates higher. Instead, the September data paints a picture of a labor market in equilibrium. Employment growth came in weaker than expected, but not weak enough to signal deterioration. For the Fed, this is the kind of data that rewards patience over action. Every month that passes without an inflation scare makes the status quo more defensible, and a rate hike harder to justify. The context matters too. Rates are already at levels the Fed considers restrictive. Adding another 25 basis points would require a clear and present threat to price stability. The September jobs report offered no such threat. The velocity suggests conviction, not noise. When markets move this far, this fast, on a single data release, it indicates a broad reassessment of the base case rather than a few large positions exiting. The January 2027 meeting had been treated as a live meeting for months, with hike probability hovering near coin-flip territory through September. That ambiguity is now resolving. A 34% implied probability means markets view a hike as possible but unlikely, a meaningful downgrade from the 48% that priced in a near-even chance just days ago. A 34% probability is not zero. The strongest case for a January 2027 hike rests on one scenario: an inflation resurgence between now and late January that forces the Fed's hand regardless of labor market stability. Two CPI reports and one PCE reading will land before the January 27 resolution date. If core inflation reaccelerates to levels that threaten the Fed's 2% target, the jobs report becomes irrelevant. The repricing from 48% to 34% captures a simple analytical conclusion: in a world where unemployment is 4.4% and wages are growing steadily, the burden of proof for a rate hike is extremely high. The Fed would need to see something materially worse in the inflation data to justify tightening into an economy that is not showing signs of overheating. The market is not saying a hike is impossible. It is saying the September jobs report moved the goalposts, and the remaining data pipeline between now and January 27 would need to deliver a surprise to move them back. At 34%, the market is pricing roughly a one-in-three chance. That feels about right for an outcome that requires a specific catalyst that has not appeared yet. The burden is now on the data to prove the market wrong.

results.title: The Fed - Monetary Policy:
highlights: On monetary policy expectations, the manager noted that market-implied expectations still indicated that market participants anticipated little change this year in the target range for the federal funds rate, and options prices implied around a 30 percent probability of a rate hike by the first quarter of 2027. In the Desk survey, the median of the modal paths continued to show two 25 basis point rate reductions over the next year, but respondents now expected them to occur later than in the previous survey, with rate cuts expected in the third or fourth quarter of 2026 and the first quarter of 2027. Staff Review of the Financial Situation Over the intermeeting period, the market-implied expected path of the federal funds rate moved up modestly, showing only a slight decline over the remainder of the year. The higher expected policy rate path was driven in part by investor concerns about the potential for near-term inflationary pressures due to the conflict in the Middle East. While both market- and survey-based measures of inflation expectations indicated upside risks to the near-term inflation outlook, measures of medium- and longer-term inflation expectations remained well anchored. In their consideration of monetary policy at this meeting, participants observed that inflation was elevated relative to the Committee's 2 percent longer-run objective, in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices. Participants generally further noted that recent indicators suggested that economic activity had been expanding at a solid pace. They also observed that job gains had remained low, on average, and that the unemployment rate had been little changed in recent months. Participants agreed that developments in the Middle East were contributing to a high level of uncertainty about the economic outlook. Against this backdrop, almost all participants supported maintaining the current target range for the federal funds rate at this meeting. Participants generally judged that the current policy rate was within the range of plausible estimates of its neutral level and that the Committee still remained well positioned to base the extent and timing of adjustments to the policy rate on incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks. They remarked that holding the policy rate steady would allow the Committee to gather additional information on how developments in the Middle East and other factors were affecting the economic outlook before determining whether adjustments to the policy rate would be warranted. One participant preferred to lower the target range for the federal funds rate 25 basis points, noting concerns that the current policy stance was overly restrictive in a situation of downside risks to the labor market. With regard to the outlook for monetary policy, participants generally judged that the continued elevated inflation readings together with uncertainty related to the duration and economic implications of the Middle East conflict could necessitate maintaining the current policy stance for longer than previously anticipated. Several participants highlighted that it would likely be appropriate to lower the target range for the federal funds rate once there are clear indications that disinflation is firmly back on track or if solid signs emerge of greater weakness in the labor market. A majority of participants highlighted, however, that some policy firming would likely become appropriate if inflation were to continue to run persistently above 2 percent. To address this possibility, many participants indicated that they would have preferred removing the language from the postmeeting statement that suggested an easing bias regarding the likely direction of the Committee's future interest rate decisions. Participants noted that monetary policy was not on a preset course and that future policy decisions would be made on a meeting-by-meeting basis. In discussing risk-management considerations bearing on the outlook for monetary policy, participants assessed that both upside risks to inflation and downside risks to employment remained elevated. Participants generally observed that the conflict in the Middle East could have significant implications for the balance of these risks and for the appropriate path of monetary policy. Several participants indicated that, in a scenario in which the conflict was resolved soon, rate reductions would be warranted later this year if the effects of higher tariffs and energy prices on inflation were to dissipate in line with their expectations. Some participants expressed concerns, however, about a scenario in which sustained elevated energy prices, combined with the effects of tariffs, could result in inflation pressures becoming embedded more broadly, potentially de-anchoring inflation expectations and creating a greater tradeoff between the Committee's employment and inflation goals. In support of the Committee's goals, almost all members agreed to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. One member voted against that decision and preferred to lower the target range by 1/4 percentage point. Nine members agreed that in considering the extent and timing of additional adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee would carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks. Three members would have preferred to provide a more two-sided characterization of the Committee's future interest rate decisions. Members agreed that the postmeeting statement should affirm their strong commitment both to supporting maximum employment and to returning inflation to the Committee's 2 percent objective. > > In support of its goals, the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-1/2 to 3-3/4 percent. highlights: The CME FedWatch Tool analyzes the probability of FOMC rate moves for upcoming meetings. Using 30-Day Fed Fund futures pricing data, which have long been relied upon to express the market’s views on the likelihood of changes in U.S. monetary policy, the tool visualizes both current and historical probabilities of various FOMC rate change outcomes for a given meeting date. The tool also shows the Fed’s “Dot Plot,” which reflects FOMC members’ expectations for the Fed target rate over time. The Fed Dot Plot, which has long reflected FOMC members’ expectations for the Fed target rate over time, is available in a chart on the CME FedWatch Tool. Each dot represents an FOMC member’s projected target rate for a given year, with the exception of the red dot, which represents the target rate implied by the year-end Fed Fund futures price for that year. Blue dots represent the FOMC members’ median rate projection. This data is also available in table format in the “Table” tab.

This one computes the probabilities independently from Fed Funds futures and then puts that read on trial against two other money crowds: prediction markets (Polymarket and Kalshi — real dollars staked on explicit outcomes) and the data itself (a Taylor-rule reaction function fed by live CPI and unemployment). When all three agree, the path is priced with conviction. When they diverge, someone is wrong — and the divergence callouts at the top tell you who is likely to blink, and in which direction the repricing runs. - Futures (what the market prices) — 30-Day Fed Funds futures (ZQ), converted meeting-by-meeting with the same methodology CME documents: when the month after a meeting has no meeting of its own, that month's contract is the post-meeting rate; otherwise the meeting month's implied average rate is solved for it. The implied move is split across the two adjacent 25bp outcomes, and the distributions chain forward across meetings. A move of more than 100bp at a single meeting is treated as a bad print and stops the chain rather than being shown. - The Taylor rule (what the data says) — r* + π + 0.5(π−2) + (u*−u) computed from live FRED CPI and unemployment. Not a forecast of the Fed — a benchmark for whether current policy is objectively tight or loose, and therefore which direction the pressure builds. - Path drift — this tool snapshots its own implied path each day it refreshes. The drift chart shows how the market's year-end view has migrated — trend in the pricing is often more tradable than the level. Snapshots whose path jumps more than 100bp between meetings are calculation artefacts, not repricing: they are never stored going forward, and any older ones are listed under the chart instead of plotted. Fed Funds futures prices come from Yahoo Finance (ZQ contracts, 15-minute cache); the current target range from FRED (DFEDTARU / DFEDTARL); FOMC dates from the Federal Reserve’s published calendar; prediction-market odds from Polymarket’s public gamma API and Kalshi’s public markets API (next meeting’s strikes near the current range; mid of bid/ask where quoted, last trade otherwise; marked unavailable when down or too thin); CPI and unemployment from FRED (CPI year-on-year matched by calendar month, so a month FRED never published can’t stretch it to 13 months). Everything recomputes on each 15-minute revalidate, and each day’s implied path is stored so the drift history accumulates.

results.title: The Fed Dot Plot: How to Read It & Why It Matters
highlights: The dot plot is the Fed’s path; the market has its own, priced through fed funds futures and read off tools such as CME FedWatch. The gap between them is a signal. A market below the dots is betting the Fed will blink; a market above them is betting inflation will force the Fed’s hand. September 2026 produced a clear example. For end-2026 the two agreed. The median dot implied one more hike; by 17 September futures priced an 87% chance of at least one and 35% odds of two. For 2027 they split. The median dot was 4.1%, meaning no further change. Yet by 24 September CME FedWatch showed 4.75% to 5.00% as the most likely range for June 2027, above every one of the 18 dots. A week after the release, futures priced about 0.75 point more tightening by mid-2027 than the median dot. Research shows how the market digests a surprise. A September 2026 Chicago Fed Letter by D’Amico, King and Torralba measured the response to a median path 25 basis points above what Fed watchers expected. Market pricing rose only about 5 basis points on the day, then about 18 basis points over the next two quarters.

results.title: Fed Funds Rate Forecast 2026-2031
highlights: Fed Funds Rate Forecast | About This Page This page provides current and historical market-based Fed Funds rate forecasts derived from futures contracts, along with the Fed's latest dot plot projection, offering insight into investor expectations and Fed guidance for monetary policy. For additional notes and data sources, continue reading below or click the info button at the top right of any chart. Comparing with the Fed Dot Plot Roughly four times a year, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) publishes a dot plot in the Summary of Economic Projections report which displays the projections of each member of the FOMC regarding the future federal funds rate. The most recent FOMC dot plot is shown here with blue dots. Each dot on the plot represents an individual FOMC member's expectation for the rate at various points in the future, usually spanning several years and including a longer-term outlook. The median of these projections often serves as an indicator of the committee's overall stance on monetary policy. The dot plot is a valuable resource for the likely trajectory of interest rates, and it can significantly influence market behavior and economic decision-making. While the dot plot serves as a key communication tool for the Fed's forward guidance, these projections provide only a snapshot of the committee's thinking at a specific moment in time. The market-based Fed Funds rate forecast continuously evolve with new economic data and changing conditions, often moving away from the Fed's most recent projections. This contrast between real-time market expectations and the Fed's quarterly guidance provides valuable insight into how market participants are interpreting economic developments and monetary policy signals. For near-term dates covered by Fed Funds futures, the chart uses daily market prices for monthly contracts. Because each contract reflects the average rate for its full calendar month, the forecast changes at scheduled FOMC meeting dates and remains level between meetings. For farther-out dates, the chart transitions to SOFR futures and connects the available market-implied rates. The stepped Fed Funds portion extends only through the near-term futures window for each quote date, so historical curves transition to longer-dated market-implied points at different calendar dates. This chart shows how the market-implied Fed Funds rate for a given date has changed over time. This allows you to track how expectations for a specific date have moved as new economic data and market conditions have changed. The Forecast Date picker can be used to choose a different point in the rate path and compare how expectations for that date evolved over the available history. Using the FOMC Meeting Timeline, you can also skip directly to future FOMC meeting rate decision dates. Methodology Notes For dates within the next year, the chart uses daily market prices for monthly Fed Funds futures. Using the known FOMC meeting dates, the implied jumps in rates are calculated. As a result, the resulting forecast changes at scheduled FOMC meeting dates and remains level between meetings. For dates farther out, SOFR futures are used and the chart uses a blended interpolation using market-implied rates.

results.title: Understanding the CME FedWatch Tool: Predicting Fed Rate Changes
highlights: How the CME FedWatch Tool Works The CME FedWatch Tool uses the prices of fed funds futures to predict how the Fed might act concerning interest rates. 2 The futures, which are traded on the CME, allow investors to speculate or hedge based on what they expect in the future direction of this key interest rate. The market prices of these contracts provide a snapshot of the collective expectations for the Fed's future moves. For example, if investors in the market expect the FOMC to raise interest rates at its next meeting, the price of the corresponding fed funds futures contract will be lower than the current rate. Meanwhile, if a rate cut is anticipated, the contract price will be higher. It's worth noting that the contract price is inversely related to the 30-day federal funds rate implied by that contract: as the price rises, the implied rate falls, and vice versa. The CME FedWatch Tool translates these market prices into probabilities, offering a succinct view of the market's expectations and assigning a probability for how much the Fed will raise, lower, or maintain the current interest rate at upcoming FOMC meetings. These probabilities help investors understand market expectations and adjust their strategies. The CME FedWatch Tool shows probabilities for Fed rate changes by 25 or 50 basis points and lets users compare them with past periods. 3 4 Source: CME Group. How to Use the CME FedWatch Tool to Analyze the Fed Dot Plot The CME FedWatch Tool incorporates a useful “dot plot” that visually represents the projected federal funds rates from the individual FOMC members for different time frames. Each dot shows an FOMC member's expected target rate, with red dots reflecting rates suggested by year-end futures prices. 4 The dot plot is a valuable resource for traders and investors, offering insights into how those investors in fed funds futures on the CME see the FOMC members' economic outlook. It also provides clues about the Fed's potential policy adjustments in response to changing economic conditions. How FOMC Expectations Affect the CME FedWatch Tool The FOMC is the branch of the Federal Reserve responsible for setting U.S. monetary policy, including the fed funds target rate. Anticipation of changes in this rate directly affects the price of Fed funds futures contracts, which then feed into the CME FedWatch Tool’s projections. The more certain the market is about the FOMC’s decision, the higher the probability assigned to that outcome by the tool. The less confident the market is, the lower the probability and the wider the range of possible outcomes. For example, if the FOMC signals that it is likely to raise the Fed’s target rate at its next meeting, then the market will adjust its expectations accordingly and bid up the price of fed funds futures contracts for that month. This will lower the implied rate and increase the probability of a rate hike by the tool. Conversely, if the FOMC indicates that is unlikely to change the ’s target rate at its next meeting, then the market will lower its expectations and bid down the price of fed funds futures contracts for that month. This will raise the implied rate and decrease the probability of a rate by the tool. Understanding the Methodology Behind the CME FedWatch Tool The approach behind the CME FedWatch Tool uses the prices of fed funds futures contracts to estimate the likelihood of rate changes. It estimates the 30-day federal funds rate from futures contracts and compares it to the FOMC's target rate. The resulting probability indicates the market's expectation for a change in the rate. 3 Fed funds futures are contracts that allow investors to speculate based on future monetary policy from the Fed. The contract price is quoted as 100 minus the implied 30-day federal funds rate. In other words, the contract price indicates what the market expects the federal funds rate to be when the contract matures. The contract price itself is not the actual cost of the contract or expressed in dollar terms. For example, if the contract price for a given month is quoted as 99.75, then the market expects the 30-day federal funds rate to be 0.25% (100.00 - 99.75) when the contract matures. The CME FedWatch Tool compares this implied rate with the target range set by the FOMC for each of its scheduled meetings. If the implied rate falls within this target range, then investors in the market collectively expect no change in the federal funds rate. Conversely, if the implied rate is either above or below the target range, that suggests that the investors anticipate a rate increase or decrease, respectively. These outcomes are standardized into increments of 25 basis points or more. The CME FedWatch Tool calculates the probability of each outcome (no change, increase, or decrease) while accounting for the market volatility and uncertainty inherent in the fed funds futures market. Probabilities are updated daily based on the latest contract prices and FOMC announcements. 3

results.title: How to Use the FedWatch Tool to Gauge Fed Policy | Charles Schwab
highlights: The FedWatch Tool is a free, real-time dashboard provided by the CME Group, a Chicago-based exchange. It offers a snapshot of market implied expectations for Fed rate moves based on 30-day Federal Funds futures (/ZQ) prices. The FedWatch Tool applies a formula based on daily trading in Fed Funds futures and then provides percentage-based probabilities on where the benchmark federal funds rate may be following each Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting during the year. It also allows traders to view the " dot-plot" of Fed officials' rate projections and compare the futures market's current rate expectations with historical data, providing a way to track shifts in market sentiment and the formal policy outlook. Select the Current tab under the Target Range subsection. Then, read the probability chart to see the odds of different rate outcomes based on futures pricing. After that, compare this data to the current target rate range to see if the futures market is expecting interest rates to fall, rise, or remain the same. In our example, the Fed's current target rate range is between 3.50% and 3.75%, and the futures market is pricing in a 78.2% probability that this won't change through December. Meanwhile, the odds of a 25-basis-point rate cut are 15.4%, and the odds of a 25-basis-point rate increase are 5.4%. Step 4: Check the dot-plot Select the Chart tab under the Dot Plot subsection to view Fed officials' latest projections for interest rates over the next few years and beyond. Compare these with the futures market's expectations to get a sense of investor sentiment and the potential for market volatility. If the market's expectations for rates clash with the Fed's, it may highlight risks in certain areas of the market. In this example, both the Fed and the futures market project rates will remain around current levels through 2026. However, it's important to remember that the Fed's dot-plot projections do not represent a commitment and are subject to change based on economic and market conditions. Even without the FedWatch Tool, traders can get a sense of the futures market's rate expectations by simply subtracting the current price of a Fed Funds futures contract from 100 and then viewing the remainder as a percentage. That percentage is an approximate estimate of what futures traders expect the fed funds rate will be in a given month. Each futures contract settles at 100 minus the average daily EFFR across all calendar days in its delivery month. For a month that contains an FOMC meeting, the month's implied average is a blend of two rates: the rate before the meeting and the rate after. Day-weighting separates them: implied_avg = (N/D) × pre_rate + ((D−N)/D) × post_rate where N = days before/on meeting day, D = total days in month. The implied change in basis points (post − pre) is then linearly interpolated across 25 bp buckets to produce the probability distribution shown in the table. Effective Federal Funds Rate The Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR) is the actual volume-weighted median rate at which U.S. depository institutions lend overnight reserve balances to one another. It is published each business day by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Fed does not set the EFFR directly — it sets a target range (e.g., 3.50%–3.75%) and uses open-market operations and the Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB) rate to keep the EFFR inside that range. In practice, the EFFR trades roughly 8–12 bp below the target upper bound — but the exact spread drifts, so this tool uses the published rate rather than an assumed offset. In the few days after an FOMC decision, before the published series catches up, the rate is instead backed out of the current-month Fed Funds contract by inverting the same day-weighting: EFFR = (implied_avg × D − post_days × post_rate) ÷ N All rate calculations on this page are denominated in the EFFR, not the target range midpoint. : Post minus pre, basis points. Green = cut priced in; red = hike; gray = effectively flat. What Is a Basis Point? A basis point (bp) is one one-hundredth of a percentage point — 0.01%. The Fed typically moves rates in 25 bp increments. A 25 bp cut from 3.75% brings the target to 3.50%. A 50 bp move (called a "jumbo" cut or hike) signals unusual urgency. Moves larger than 50 bp are historically rare outside emergency conditions. On this page, >25bp cut/hike means the market is pricing a move larger than one standard increment.
